Also, consider whether talking with a counselor or therapist might help — they can offer personalized tools, especially if this pattern feels deeply rooted or connected to other struggles.

Be patient with yourself. Changing thought patterns takes time, and setbacks don't mean you're failing. The fact that you want to grow in this way says a lot about your self-awareness and resilience.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response:
I'm so sorry you're dealing with all of this — racing thoughts, poor sleep, and anxiety after a head injury is an exhausting combination, and it's especially frustrating when medication options haven't worked for you. Since you've had strong physical reactions to medications, it's important to talk with your doctor about those specific side effects so they can explore alternatives or non-medication approaches that may be gentler on your system.

In the meantime, some people find relief with grounding techniques like slow box breathing — inhale for four counts, hold four, exhale four, hold four — which can help calm your nervous system without any side effects. Progressive muscle relaxation, where you tense and release muscle groups one at a time, may also help with both anxiety and sleep. Reducing screen time before bed, keeping your room cool and dark, and trying a guided sleep meditation can make a difference too. You might also ask your doctor about whether a referral to a neuropsychologist or a therapist experienced with brain injury could be helpful — there are therapy approaches that don't involve medication at all. You're not alone in this, and it's okay to keep searching for what works for you.

prompt: I been having anger problems a lot lately. It only takes one word wrongly said to set me off. I use to not be like this until I got with my soon-to-be husband. I think his mood and rage/anger problems have rubbed off on me a lot. I don't get nearly as bad as he does, but I yell almost constantly and I can't seem to just stop. I have two young babies that have to hear this, and I don't want my girls growing up with a mommy like I have been lately. I just don't know how to get back to my old self.
response:
It takes real courage to recognize this pattern and want to change it, especially with your girls in mind. That self-awareness is actually a powerful first step. It's also very possible that living in a high-conflict environment is affecting you more than you realize—we often absorb the stress and emotional patterns around us.

You might find it helpful to explore individual counseling, where you can process what you're experiencing and develop tools for managing those intense reactions. Couples counseling could also be valuable, especially if your fiancé is open to addressing his anger. If you ever feel unsafe or worried about escalating conflict, please reach out to a domestic violence hotline like 1-800-799-7233—they support people in many types of difficult relationship dynamics, not just physical situations. Your girls deserve a peaceful home, and so do you.

prompt: My four year old daughter has been struggling with her milestones for as long as I can remember. Potty training has been an absolute nightmare, she refuses to go and will even sit on the toilet crying for half an hour while refusing to "go" at all. In fact she's never once used the toilet correctly. She gestures at herself in the mirror, looking at herself is one of her favorite hobbies, but anytime one of us is looking at her it feels like she's looking through us instead of at us. We were hoping that a half day at preschool would be helpful for her to develop out of these issues but they seem to persist. What can we try next?
response:
It sounds like you've been working incredibly hard to support your daughter, and it's understandable to feel worried when milestones aren't unfolding the way you'd hoped. You clearly know her well and are paying close attention, which matters a lot.

The pattern you're describing—the significant difficulty with potty training, the challenges around eye contact, and milestones that have persisted despite preschool—are things worth discussing with a professional who can actually evaluate her. I'd encourage you to talk with your pediatrician and ask specifically about a developmental evaluation. In many areas you can also request an assessment through early intervention or your local school district, often at no cost. The earlier a child gets tailored support, the more effective it tends to be.

In the meantime, try to ease the pressure around the toilet so it doesn't become a source of distress for either of you. You're doing the right thing by seeking answers, and getting the right people involved is the strongest next step you can take.

prompt: I am on social security and have a budget. My son has been coming over the house to help with some work that needs to be done, and I think Im missing money,. It has to be him, no one else comes over and knows where i keep my money. I am going to confront him.
response:
That sounds really stressful, especially when you're on a fixed budget and every dollar matters. It's understandable to feel hurt and worried, particularly because this involves your son and someone you trust.

Before you confront him, it might help to be sure of what's actually missing. Could you keep a written record of exactly how much you have and when, so you have something concrete to point to? When you do talk with him, try leading with what you've noticed rather than an accusation—something like, "I've noticed some money missing and I'm confused about it." That can open a conversation instead of putting him on the defensive, and it leaves room in case the explanation isn't what you expect. If it turns out money is being taken, you deserve support in protecting yourself. Whatever happens, your feelings here are valid, and I hope the conversation brings you some clarity.

prompt: I have four children. One of them is in her 20s, and she cannot afford to go, nor can I pay for her. She went last year for two weeks by herself.
response:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of guilt or worry about not being able to provide something for your daughter, even though she's an adult who managed on her own last year. That kind of pressure can weigh heavily on a parent, especially when finances are tight and you have four children to think about.

It might help to remember that your love and support aren't measured by what you can pay for. Your daughter is in her 20s and has already shown she can navigate things independently. Being honest with her about what's realistic right now is not a failure—it's part of a healthy adult relationship. If you'd like, it may help to talk openly with her about the situation together, so the responsibility doesn't feel like it rests only on you.

Is there a particular part of this that's troubling you most? I'm happy to listen.

prompt: Sometimes I feel like I shouldn’t be this upset because other people have gone through worse. I can’t stop having flashbacks, and I think about the past constantly. I don’t know why I’m still stuck in it. I haven’t been through anything that bad. Am I being dramatic?
response:
You're not being dramatic. What you're describing—flashbacks and constantly thinking about the past—sounds genuinely painful, and your mind and body are responding to something that affected you. Pain isn't a competition; what matters is that you're hurting and having a hard time coping, and that's real regardless of how your experiences compare to anyone else's.

It's very common to minimize what we've been through, especially when intrusive memories make us feel like we should just "get over it." But healing isn't about willpower, and being stuck doesn't mean you're weak or exaggerating. It often means you're carrying something that hasn't been fully processed yet. A mental health professional could help you understand what's happening and work through it at your own pace—you deserve support for what you're experiencing, not judgment.

prompt: I was “mentored” by this guy for a few years spiritually. It was okay at times, but other times, it was just weird. I try not to think about it too much, but a lot of manipulation and lying happened, yet no one else really believed me when I told them. It's like he's two different people, and no one else really sees that side of him. I was blamed for a lot of our troubles, and now we don't really talk much. I'm worried because he's in a trusted position of leadership and no one suspects anything. They just think I'm attacking his character. How do I know for sure?
response:
It's really painful when you've experienced manipulation and then others dismiss or doubt your account. What you're describing—someone presenting differently to others than they did to you, being blamed for problems, and feeling confused about what was real—are common experiences in manipulative relationships. The fact that others don't see it doesn't mean it didn't happen; many people who cause harm are skilled at maintaining a positive public image.

You don't need absolute certainty or external validation to trust your own experience. You lived it. You felt the impact. Writing down specific memories—what happened, how you felt—can help you reconnect with your own perspective rather than relying on others' interpretations. Consider talking with a counselor who understands spiritual or relational manipulation; they can help you process this without pressure to "prove" anything. Your concern about others potentially being affected is valid, but your primary responsibility is your own healing and wellbeing right now.

prompt: I have a very negative relationship with my mother. She is often overbearing, demanding too much from me, and treating me like a servant. I thought this would get easier when I moved out of the house but she still calls me constantly and comes over unexpectedly at least twice a week. Every favor from her comes with strings attached but she expects me to drop everything and do any favor I can for her constantly. How can I put my foot down in a way that she'll respect?
response:
It makes sense you're frustrated—moving out was supposed to give you space, and instead the demands followed you. That's exhausting.

With someone who's used to unlimited access, respect usually comes from consistency, not from finding the perfect words. You might set a few clear boundaries: choosing when you answer calls, letting her know you need advance notice before visits, and saying no to favors that have strings attached. Try stating these calmly and briefly—"I can't do that this week" or "Please call before coming over"—without over-explaining, since explanations often invite negotiation. Expect pushback at first; that's normal, and holding steady is what eventually shifts the pattern.

You won't always control her reaction, only your own follow-through. It can also help to decide in advance what you'll do if she ignores a boundary, like not opening the door for an unannounced visit. If this feels overwhelming, talking with a therapist could help you build a plan that fits your relationship.

prompt: I am a teacher who sees one of your clients. I am worried that they are experiencing anxiety all the time and seem to have a low distress tolerance threshold. I think you should talk to her mom about getting medication.
response:
It sounds like you care deeply about your student and want to help her get the support she needs. I'm not a therapist or mental health provider, so I'm not able to contact her family or make recommendations about medication. However, your observations are valuable, and there are steps you can take.

Consider sharing your concerns with the school counselor, psychologist, or administration, as they can follow appropriate protocols to reach out to the family and connect them with qualified professionals. If you have direct contact with her mom, you could also gently share what you've noticed in the classroom and suggest she consult with their pediatrician or a mental health specialist. Only a qualified medical or mental health professional can assess whether medication or other interventions might be appropriate.

Thank you for looking out for your student's wellbeing. Teachers are often the first to notice when a child is struggling, and your attentiveness can make a real difference.

prompt: How do I stop thinking so irrationally about death? It controls my entire life and stops me from doing fun things. I want to be able to live my life to the fullest without thinking of death all time.
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to have the fear of death constantly overshadowing your life and keeping you from the things you enjoy. When these intrusive thoughts take over, it can be helpful to practice grounding techniques to bring your focus back to the present moment. Try focusing on your immediate senses—what you can see, hear, or feel right now—to gently guide your mind away from the "what ifs" and back to the present activity.

Since these thoughts are controlling your entire life, reaching out to a mental health professional could be incredibly beneficial. Therapies like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) are specifically designed to help you identify, challenge, and reframe irrational fears so they lose their power over you. You deserve to live fully and enjoy your life, and with the right support and tools, it is absolutely possible to quiet these thoughts and reclaim your joy.

prompt: My son and daughter in law had a baby who is 4 weeks old now. They have not invited me to come over and see the baby since I saw him in the hospital. I did not have a good relationship with my son once he became an adult because we did not agree on the lifestyle he was living. I was under the impression that we had made up and things were better but apparently not. I am guess I am supposed to sit around and wait on him to call me and give me permission to be in their lives? This is very upsetting and I don’t like being left out like this.
response:
It's completely understandable that you're feeling hurt and left out. Wanting to be part of your grandson's life is a natural and loving desire, and the silence from your son is painful, especially given your history.

The first few weeks with a newborn are often overwhelming for new parents, and they may simply be exhausted or focused on adjusting. That said, your feelings matter too. Rather than waiting and building resentment, consider reaching out with a gentle, low-pressure message — something like expressing love for them and the baby, acknowledging this is a busy time, and letting them know you'd love to visit when they're ready. Keep it warm and avoid rehashing past conflicts. This approach shows you respect their boundaries while also expressing your desire to be involved. If they don't respond positively, you may need to accept their timeline, but taking the first step with kindness can help open the door. If the emotional weight becomes too heavy, talking with a counselor could help you process these feelings.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response:
Generally, no—not without your permission. Therapists are bound by confidentiality rules (like HIPAA in the U.S.), so a past therapist cannot share your information with a current one unless you provide written consent, usually through a signed release-of-information form.

If you'd like your two therapists to coordinate care, you can request that yourself, and you get to decide what information is shared. There are limited exceptions where disclosure may happen without consent—such as a serious safety risk or a legal requirement—but routine sharing between providers requires your authorization. If you have concerns about your specific situation, it's worth asking your current therapist directly about their confidentiality policies. They should be able to walk you through your options and rights.

prompt: I have a close friend who started to stand me up after I disclosed my feelings for him. When I initially disclosed these feelings he said that nothing would change between us as far as our friendship but he didn’t want to explore a romantic relationship. When I try to reach out to him to talk about it, he doesn’t want to address it. I feel like this is not fair because he told me it would be fine. I want me friend back, I don’t know what to do.
response:
That sounds really painful—you took a risk by being honest, he promised things wouldn't change, and now his actions are telling a different story. Feeling hurt and confused by that gap between his words and behavior makes complete sense.

The hard truth is that you can control your own openness, but not whether he chooses to show up. You might try one calm, direct message naming what you've noticed: that you value the friendship and feel disappointed he seems to be pulling away, and asking if you can talk honestly about where things stand. If he still avoids it, that itself is an answer, even if not the one you wanted. Sometimes friendships need space after a disclosure like this, and sometimes people aren't as capable of staying close as they hoped they'd be.

Whatever he decides, be gentle with yourself. You didn't do anything wrong by sharing your feelings, and you deserve friends who can meet you honestly.

prompt: I would like to be able to have more positive relationships in the present.
response:
It is wonderful that you are focusing on building more positive relationships right now. Recognizing that desire is a great first step toward creating meaningful and fulfilling connections in your life. To foster healthier relationships, it can help to start by reflecting on what "positive" means to you—whether that involves mutual respect, open communication, or shared interests.

Setting clear boundaries and practicing active listening are powerful ways to nurture trust and understanding with others. Remember that building strong connections takes time and patience. Being kind to yourself and showing up authentically will naturally draw people who appreciate and support you for who you are.

prompt: My wife recently lost a great deal of weight due to a weight loss drug. She is going out, staying out late, not answering her phone, and being distant. I do not want to live like this and I am thinking of leaving her. What do you think?
response:
It sounds incredibly painful and confusing to watch your wife change so drastically, not just physically but in how she relates to you. When a partner suddenly becomes distant, ignores your calls, and starts living a separate life, it is completely understandable that you would feel hurt and question the future of your marriage. You deserve to feel valued, respected, and connected in your relationship.

Before making a final decision about leaving, you might consider having a direct and honest conversation with her about how her actions are impacting you and the marriage. If she is unwilling to communicate or if the distance continues, couples counseling or individual therapy could help you navigate this difficult transition. Ultimately, the decision to leave is deeply personal and only yours to make, but seeking professional guidance can provide you with support and clarity on the best path forward for your own well-being.

prompt: My girlfriend seems to always be on the go -- rarely sleeping, hardly eating, always talking about her dreams and aspirations. She makes time for fitness and work, but doesn't seem able to stay on task for much else. It harms our relationship, and I'm wondering if this could be a sign of bipolar disorder?
response:
It sounds like you care deeply about your girlfriend and are understandably concerned about how her behavior is affecting her well-being and your relationship. The behaviors you described—such as a significantly decreased need for sleep, high energy, intense focus on big aspirations, and difficulty staying on task—can sometimes be associated with manic or hypomanic episodes, which are characteristic of bipolar disorder. However, these symptoms can also be linked to other medical or mental health conditions, such as severe stress, anxiety, or thyroid issues.

Because only a qualified healthcare professional can provide an accurate evaluation, the best step is to gently encourage her to speak with a doctor or a therapist. You might approach the conversation by focusing on your care for her overall health and how you want to support her, rather than mentioning a specific diagnosis right away. Remember to also take care of yourself and consider seeking your own support, as navigating a partner's health challenges can be very stressful.

prompt: My wife is always accusing me of cheating and telling me that I'm doing things she finds disrespectful even when I don't mean it like that. For example, she gets offended when I call someone at work "sweetheart." I wish I had a penny for every time she accused me of cheating on her. She doesn't, and never will say she was wrong. How do I get her to understand?
response:
It sounds exhausting to feel constantly accused and misunderstood, especially when you don't intend any harm. That kind of ongoing tension can really wear on a person over time.

One thing worth considering: you can't force someone to admit they're wrong, but you can shift how you communicate. Instead of trying to "win" the point, try naming the impact—something like, "When I'm accused of cheating and I've done nothing, I feel hurt and it distances me from you." That focuses on connection rather than blame. It may also help to gently ask what's driving her fears; sometimes accusations come from insecurity or past wounds rather than anything you've done.

If the accusations, monitoring, or controlling behavior feel persistent, a couples counselor can offer a neutral space to work through it together. And it's worth reflecting honestly on whether this dynamic feels healthy for you overall. What feels like the hardest part for you right now?

prompt: How do I cope with losing my mom?
response:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your mom. Grief this deep reflects how much she meant to you, and there's no right way or timeline for moving through it. Some days may feel unbearable, others a little lighter—both are normal.

Be gentle with yourself. Let the feelings come rather than forcing them away, and lean on people who care about you when you can. Small routines, rest, and even talking about her or holding onto meaningful memories can help you feel connected to her. If the pain feels overwhelming or you find it hard to function, consider reaching out to a grief counselor or support group—many people find real comfort in sharing with others who understand.

And if you ever feel hopeless or like you might harm yourself, please reach out right away to a crisis line or someone you trust. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: I keep on begging him to come back. I am so unhappy with him but am so scared of being a single parent to our son. I was abused as a little girl and that has made to be very abusive to men. What should I do...
response:
It takes a lot of courage to recognize how your past trauma is affecting your present behavior. It is completely understandable to feel terrified at the thought of being a single parent, but begging someone to return to an unhappy dynamic won't heal the underlying pain for either of you, or create a healthy environment for your son.

The most important step you can take right now is to seek professional support. A therapist or counselor can help you process the childhood abuse you endured, learn healthier ways to cope with those deep wounds, and break the cycle of abusive behavior. Working on your own healing is the best way to build a safe, stable future for both you and your son, whether you are co-parenting or navigating life on your own.

prompt: My new high school is incredibly cliquey. Seems like everyone belongs to a tight group and every group wants nothing to do with the others. I'm definitely not a jock or a nerd so now I'm feeling pressure to join the theater kids. I think I want to start my own group: "The Normal Ones." After all, what's wrong with just being normal these days?
response:
It sounds like starting fresh at a new school has been really overwhelming, and it's completely understandable to feel like you don't fit into the existing boxes everyone else seems to occupy. High school social scenes can feel rigid and exhausting, especially when you're the new person trying to find your footing.

There's absolutely nothing wrong with being "normal" — or more accurately, being someone who doesn't neatly fit into a labeled category. That's actually most people, even if it doesn't look that way from the outside. Starting your own group or simply finding one or two people you genuinely connect with is a great approach. You don't need to force yourself into a clique that doesn't feel authentic just to belong somewhere. Give it time, stay open to unexpected friendships, and remember that the right people will appreciate you for exactly who you are.

prompt: My partner is going through severe mental health issues and has made several comments about being suicidal when in arguments. If I try to take space for myself or set boundaries with them, they threaten suicide. I don't want them to hurt themselves, but I need to take care of myself. What do I do?
response:
This is an incredibly hard situation, and it makes sense that you feel torn between caring for your partner and protecting yourself. Please know that you can do both—caring about someone doesn't mean you're responsible for keeping them alive, and setting boundaries isn't what causes a person to harm themselves.

When someone mentions suicide, it's important to take it seriously. If you believe they're in immediate danger, contact emergency services (911 in the US) or a crisis line like 988 (US) where you can also get guidance on how to respond. At the same time, threats used to prevent you from taking space aren't something you can safely manage alone—their safety ultimately requires professional support, not your constant availability.

You deserve support too. Consider reaching out to a therapist for yourself, and remember you're allowed to step away, rest, and set limits. You matter in this, and taking care of yourself isn't a betrayal of them.

prompt: Sometimes I can't stop eating. I get so hungry all the time, and no matter how hard I try, I just keep on eating, long after I'm full. I always regret it afterwards. Is something wrong with me?
response:
What you're describing sounds really difficult, and the cycle of eating past fullness followed by regret can feel exhausting and isolating. Please know you're not "broken"—many people struggle with patterns like this, and it doesn't mean something is wrong with who you are. Sometimes intense hunger and overeating can be tied to physical factors, emotions, stress, or restrictive eating patterns, and it's often more complex than just willpower.

Because there can be both physical and emotional pieces to this, it might help to talk with a doctor or a registered dietitian who can look at what's going on for you specifically. A therapist experienced with eating concerns can also be really valuable if food feels tied to your emotions. Being gentle with yourself matters too—the regret cycle tends to grow harsher when we judge ourselves. You reached out and named this honestly, which takes real courage, and it's a meaningful first step toward feeling better.

prompt: I am extremely possessive in my relationships and this is hurting my friendships. How can I fix my underlying issues?
response:
It takes real self-awareness and courage to recognize this pattern and want to change it. Possessiveness often stems from deeper fears—like fear of abandonment, insecurity, or anxiety about losing connection. These feelings are valid, but acting on them in ways that push people away can create a painful cycle.

A good starting point is to notice the thoughts and physical sensations that arise when you feel possessive urges. Are you afraid someone will leave? Do you feel you're not enough? Therapy can be incredibly helpful for unpacking these root causes and building healthier relationship patterns. In the moment, practicing pausing before reacting, challenging anxious thoughts, and allowing your friends space without trying to control their choices can help you respond differently over time. Change is absolutely possible with patience and practice.

prompt: Can a therapist have a client admitted to an eating disorder treatment center if the client does not want to go?
response:
It is understandable to feel anxious about the possibility of forced treatment. In most places, a therapist cannot simply force a client into an eating disorder treatment center against their will. Involuntary admission is generally considered a last resort and involves a strict legal and medical process. It typically only happens if a person is in immediate, severe, and life-threatening medical danger—such as acute organ failure or severe malnutrition—and is deemed unable to make safe decisions for themselves.

Because laws regarding involuntary holds vary significantly by location, a therapist usually has to work with medical doctors, hospitals, or the legal system to initiate this process; they cannot do it alone. If you are worried about this, it can be very helpful to share your fears directly with your therapist. Their primary goal is almost always to work collaboratively with you to keep you safe and support your recovery in the least restrictive environment possible.

prompt: I have major depression, severe, PTSD, anxiety disorder, and personality disorder. I had an appointment with my doctor. I was very upset, and I shared with him about that particular drug.
response:
It sounds like you were carrying a lot into that appointment, and it took courage to bring up your concerns about that medication with your doctor. Living with several conditions at once can feel overwhelming, and being upset in that moment makes complete sense.

I want to make sure I understand you well—would you like to share what happened after you told him, or what's weighing on you most right now? If you're having thoughts of harming yourself or feeling unsafe, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. Otherwise, I'm here to listen and think this through with you.

prompt: My new daughter-in-law just informed me that she is smoking marijuana while pregnant because of her morning sickness. I’m in shock and I don’t know how to respond. I just lost my mom, and she was good with advice.
response:
I am so sorry for the loss of your mother. It is completely understandable that you are feeling overwhelmed and missing her wisdom right now, especially when faced with such a surprising and delicate situation. It is natural to be deeply concerned about your grandchild's health and your daughter-in-law's choices.

When you feel ready to talk to her, try to approach the conversation from a place of love and concern rather than judgment. You might gently acknowledge how miserable severe morning sickness can be, and encourage her to speak honestly with her OB/GYN. Doctors can offer safe, prescription alternatives to help manage nausea during pregnancy. By keeping the lines of communication open and focusing on her well-being and the baby's health, you can offer support while gently guiding her toward professional medical advice. Take your time to process your own shock and grief first, so you can have this conversation calmly when you are ready.

prompt: How can I make my thoughts stop? Are there any ways to make my anxiety stop fast?
response:
It sounds like you're feeling really overwhelmed right now, and I want you to know that's a painful but understandable place to be. While we can't simply switch thoughts off, there are techniques that can help quiet them. Try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding method: name five things you see, four you can touch, three you hear, two you smell, and one you taste. This pulls your attention into the present moment. Slow, deep breathing—inhaling for four counts, holding for four, exhaling for four—can also calm your nervous system fairly quickly.

If your anxiety feels unmanageable, you're experiencing distressing thoughts that won't stop, or you feel unsafe, please reach out to a crisis line like 988 (in the U.S.) or contact a healthcare professional. You deserve support, and you don't have to struggle through this alone.

prompt: "I’ve been feeling really depressed for weeks and can’t get out of bed. I don’t want therapy because it hasn’t helped in the past. What medication do you think would work for me?"
response:
I'm so sorry you've been dealing with this heavy depression and struggling to get out of bed. It is completely understandable that you feel frustrated with therapy if it hasn't worked for you in the past, and it makes sense that you are looking for other ways to find relief.

Because I am an AI, I cannot recommend or prescribe specific medications. Finding the right medication depends on many personal factors, including your medical history, genetics, and specific symptoms. Reaching out to a psychiatrist or your primary care doctor is the best next step. They can listen to your experiences, respect your boundaries regarding therapy, and work with you to explore medication options that might help lift this heavy weight. You don't have to figure this out all on your own, and a medical professional can help guide you toward a treatment that fits your needs.

prompt: My parents have always been difficult to deal with, and never supported me emotionally. I don't have a close relationship with them, and I don't want to visit over the holidays -- but I am worried as to what this might do if I didn't attend. What should I do?
response:
It's completely valid to protect your emotional well-being, especially when a relationship has historically been unsupportive. You're allowed to set boundaries, and choosing not to visit doesn't make you a bad person — it may be an important act of self-care.

That said, it's worth thinking through what you're worried about specifically. Are you concerned about guilt, family conflict, or social pressure? Naming those fears can help you decide what feels right. You might consider alternatives — a shorter visit, setting clear time limits, or connecting by phone instead. Or you might decide that skipping this year is the healthiest choice for you.

Whatever you decide, try to plan something nurturing for yourself during the holidays so you aren't left feeling isolated. If you have a trusted friend, therapist, or support group, talking it through with someone who knows your situation can help you feel more confident in your decision. There's no single "right" answer — just the one that best honors your needs and emotional safety.

prompt: You are meeting with a woman that alleges spousal abuse by her husband (verbal and physical). She shares that he would like to join in on future sessions in an effort to repair the relationship, and your client is amenable to this. Would you allow the husband to join in on a session?
response:
This is an important clinical and ethical question. Generally, best practices in the field caution against couples therapy when there is alleged ongoing abuse, as joint sessions can risk the victim's safety, increase retaliation, and be used by the abuser to manipulate the narrative. A client's willingness to include her husband may also reflect coercion or fear rather than genuine choice.

The priority should be the client's safety and autonomy. Individual sessions should continue, and any consideration of joint work would typically require a thorough risk assessment, the client's freely given informed consent, and ideally referral to a provider specially trained in domestic violence dynamics. Many experts recommend that the alleged abuser pursue his own individual therapy first. If you are facing this situation in a professional capacity, consulting with a supervisor or a domestic violence specialist would be advisable before making any decision.

prompt: My husband doesn’t trust me for some past we had. I know all marriages have their ups and downs, but sometimes, I feel I am getting tired of the same thing over and over: that I am messing around, which I am not.
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to repeatedly face accusations when you're doing your best to rebuild trust. Your feelings of fatigue are completely valid — trust takes time to repair, but it also requires both partners to actively work toward healing, not just one person constantly defending themselves.

Consider having an open, calm conversation with your husband about how these recurring accusations are affecting you and the marriage. Couples counseling could provide a safe space to address the root of his mistrust and develop healthier communication patterns together. You deserve to feel believed and respected in your relationship.

prompt: "I feel like everyone around me is happy, confident, and knows what they’re doing, and I’m the only one who feels empty and fake all the time. Is it normal to feel like nothing matters even though I have a good life?"
response:
What you're describing is more common than it feels right now. Many people who seem confident and put-together are quietly struggling too—we tend to compare our messy inner experience to everyone else's polished outside, which makes us feel uniquely broken when we're really not. Feeling empty or like nothing matters, even when your life looks "good" on paper, is something a lot of people go through, and it doesn't mean you're fake or ungrateful.

That said, when that emptiness sticks around and dulls the things that used to matter, it can be a sign that something deeper is worth paying attention to. It might help to talk with a doctor or therapist who can help you understand what's going on and feel more like yourself again. If you ever reach a point where you're thinking about harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You deserve support with this.

prompt: I self-harm, and I stop for awhile. Then when I see something sad or depressing, I automatically want to self-harm.
response:
Thank you for sharing this. It takes a lot of courage to talk about self-harm. It is very common for the urge to return when you encounter sad or distressing triggers, as your mind may have learned to use self-harm as an automatic coping mechanism for emotional pain. The fact that you are recognizing this pattern—and that you have been able to stop for periods of time—shows incredible strength and self-awareness.

Because your safety is so important, please consider reaching out for support to help navigate these triggers. You can connect with people who care and want to help by texting HOME to 741741 to reach the Crisis Text Line, or by calling or texting 988 (in the US and Canada) for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Please be gentle with yourself right now, and know that free, confidential support is available whenever those urges arise.

prompt: My best friend passed away unexpectedly 7 years ago. I still miss him, and cry every day. I know it is not normal, but I dint know how to stop. What do you think ,might help?
response:
I am so sorry for the unexpected loss of your best friend. Losing someone so close leaves a profound impact, and it makes complete sense that you still miss him deeply. While grief doesn't have a set expiration date, crying every day after seven years sounds incredibly exhausting and painful. Please be gentle with yourself. There is no "normal" way to grieve, but you don't have to carry this heavy burden all on your own.

When grief remains this intense for a long time, speaking with a grief counselor or a therapist can be incredibly beneficial. A professional can provide a safe space to process these overwhelming emotions and help you find gentle ways to integrate this loss into your life. They can guide you in honoring your friend's memory while also finding a path forward so that the pain doesn't consume your everyday life. You deserve support, comfort, and healing.

prompt: Lately I have been feeling very fatigued, my hair is falling out, I have gained weight and some more concerning symptoms. My husband says it’s most likely my depression and although that might be somewhat true I think something else is going on. Every time I tell him that I think it’s more than depression, he tells me I wrong. Is he gaslighting me?
response:
It sounds incredibly frustrating to experience those physical symptoms and feel like your concerns are being dismissed. When someone repeatedly invalidates your reality or tells you that your experiences are wrong, it can certainly feel like gaslighting, regardless of their intent. Your body is yours, and you are the expert on how you feel.

While symptoms like fatigue, hair loss, and weight gain can sometimes be linked to depression, they are also very common signs of underlying medical conditions. It is important to trust your instincts and consult a healthcare professional who can run tests and give you a proper medical evaluation. You deserve to have your symptoms taken seriously and to get to the bottom of what you are experiencing, even if your husband doesn't agree. Please consider making an appointment with a doctor to advocate for your health and get the answers you need.

prompt: Sometimes I feel like I shouldn’t be this upset because other people have gone through worse. I can’t stop having flashbacks, and I think about the past constantly. I don’t know why I’m still stuck in it. I haven’t been through anything that bad. Am I being dramatic?
response:
You are not being dramatic. It is very common to minimize our own pain by comparing it to what others have experienced, but trauma and distress are not a competition. Your feelings are completely valid, regardless of how your experiences measure up to someone else's. The fact that you are having flashbacks and constant intrusive thoughts shows that whatever you went through had a profound impact on you, and your mind is still trying to process it.

Feeling stuck in the past is incredibly exhausting, and you don't have to navigate this alone. Because flashbacks can be so overwhelming, it could be very helpful to speak with a mental health professional. They can help you understand why your brain is holding onto these memories and provide tools to help you find relief and move forward. Your pain deserves care and attention, no matter what caused it.

prompt: I know that I need to get past my feelings for this person I fell in love with, but t's so difficult to move on because he showed me feelings I've never felt before. I feel like I don't want to be without my genuine love for him, but logically, I know I need to be without him. I can't discuss this with anybody in my life because the conditions surrounding our love are considered "wrong" by a lot of people. How can I get myself to just move on?
response:
It makes sense that this feels so hard. When someone opens up feelings in us we've never experienced before, letting go isn't just about the person—it's about grieving a part of ourselves that came alive with them. That's a real loss, and it deserves patience rather than pressure to "just move on."

You don't have to force yourself to stop caring; that genuine love was real, and honoring it isn't the same as staying attached. Moving on tends to happen gradually as you build a life full enough that the space he occupied slowly fills with other meaningful things. And carrying this alone, especially when you fear judgment, adds another layer of pain. A therapist offers a completely confidential, non-judgmental space where you could talk through the details you can't share elsewhere—that might ease some of the isolation. You deserve support with this, not shame. Be gentle with yourself; healing from something this significant takes time.

prompt: How do counselors navigate working with a minor with parents who are divorced? Do both parents have to agree for the child to come to therapy? I want to bring my child without including my ex-spouse.
response:
This is a common and understandable question, and the answer depends largely on where you live and your custody arrangement.

Generally, consent to treat a minor is tied to legal custody, not physical custody. If you have sole legal custody, you can typically consent to therapy on your own. If you and your ex share joint legal custody, most states and most counselors require consent from both parents before beginning treatment—so it's worth reviewing your custody order and being prepared for that possibility. Laws vary by state and country, so it may help to consult your custody agreement or a family law attorney for specifics.

When you're ready, I'd encourage you to speak directly with the counselor's office; they handle these situations regularly and can walk you through their specific consent requirements. If your goal is to support your child through the challenges of the divorce, that's a caring step, and the counselor can help you find the right path forward.

prompt: My mother takes care of niece whom my sister abandoned. She calls me every day complaining, but I don't want to hear it anymore.
response:
It's completely valid to feel this way. You're not responsible for absorbing all your mother's stress, and setting boundaries doesn't mean you don't care about her or your niece. Caregiver burnout is real, and it sounds like your mother may need more support than daily venting can provide.

You might try gently letting her know you love her but find the daily complaints difficult, and ask if you can focus your calls on other topics. You could also encourage her to seek support through caregiver groups, respite care services, or counseling—local family services or organizations like the National Alliance for Caregiving may have resources. If your niece's situation involves legal custody or child welfare concerns, your mother might benefit from consulting a family law attorney or local social services. Taking care of your own mental health matters too, so consider reaching out to a counselor if you're feeling overwhelmed by the family dynamics.

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response:
Great question—strong relationships take intentional effort over time. A few things tend to make a real difference: keeping communication open and honest, especially about the hard topics like money, intimacy, and expectations. Couples who do well often learn to argue fairly—focusing on the issue rather than attacking each other, and taking breaks when things get heated. Showing appreciation regularly and making time for connection, even in small ways, helps couples stay emotionally close rather than drifting into just "roommates."

It also helps to keep growing together, supporting each other's individual goals while building shared ones. When bigger struggles come up, seeking help early—like couples counseling—can prevent small problems from becoming large ones. Reaching out isn't a sign of failure; it's a sign you value the relationship.

If you're asking because something specific is weighing on you or your partner right now, I'm glad to talk through it more. What's on your mind?

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response:
Reducing the risk of divorce often comes down to consistent, intentional effort in the relationship. Couples who stay connected tend to prioritize open communication, making time to really listen to each other without judgment. They also work on managing conflict constructively—addressing issues directly rather than letting resentment build, and being willing to repair after disagreements rather than staying withdrawn.

It's also important to nurture friendship and appreciation within the partnership. Small gestures of kindness, expressing gratitude, and making space for shared activities can strengthen the emotional bond over time. Being realistic about challenges and willing to seek support—whether through couples counseling or trusted resources—can also make a meaningful difference. Every relationship faces difficulties, and reaching out for help early rather than waiting until things feel overwhelming is a sign of strength, not failure.

prompt: My child is dealing with depression and has suicidal thoughts but I had a really bad experience taking Zoloft, and I don't want my child to be on Zoloft. Are there other options, or should we just not consider medication?
response:
I understand your concern, and it's natural to feel worried given your own experience with Zoloft. Your child's response to any medication could be very different from yours, and there are many treatment options beyond Zoloft that a child psychiatrist or prescribing doctor can consider. Medication can be an important part of treatment, especially when suicidal thoughts are present, but this decision should be made with a qualified healthcare provider who can evaluate your child's specific needs.

Given that your child is experiencing suicidal thoughts, please reach out to their doctor or a mental health professional as soon as possible, or contact a crisis line if needed. You can call or text 988 in the US anytime. A professional can help you explore all options, including therapy, medication, or a combination, and monitor your child's safety. You're doing the right thing by seeking information and support.

prompt: If a parent asks a counselor to share every detail of session with them after every single appointment with their child, is the counselor ethically allowed to do so? If not, what information can they share?
response:
Generally, no—a counselor typically cannot share every detail of a child's sessions, even with a requesting parent. While parents often have legal rights to their minor child's records, most ethical guidelines encourage counselors to protect a child's confidentiality to preserve trust, which is essential for effective therapy. This is especially true for older children and teens.

In practice, counselors often share general information rather than specific details—things like themes being worked on, treatment goals, overall progress, and any safety concerns. Many counselors set clear boundaries at the start of treatment, sometimes with an agreement about what will and won't be shared. Important exceptions do exist: if a child is at risk of harming themselves or others, or if there's suspected abuse, the counselor is obligated to disclose that.

Exact rules vary by state and by the specific ethical code (like the ACA or APA). If you're navigating this, it's worth asking the counselor directly about their confidentiality policy—they should be willing to explain their approach.

prompt: My son has struggled with his extreme hyper "zoomies" (as we call them) for as long as any of us can remember. Ever since he was walking he wouldn't stop. He beats to his own drum and none of us can keep up. We put him in all kind of sports after school but surprisingly he doesn't seem to love any of them. Right now is basketball season and my husband and I can tell he isn't enjoying himself, but its just so helpful that he comes home wore out. Any day he goes to bed before 11pm is a miracle to us. Are we wrong for making him do sports to get his zoomies out?
response:
It sounds like you're doing your best to support a very energetic kid while also protecting everyone's sanity—that's a real balancing act, and you're clearly thinking about what he needs.

You're not "wrong" for wanting an outlet for his energy, but it's worth noticing that the goal has shifted a bit from *him enjoying an activity* to *him being worn out*. Those don't always overlap. Some kids thrive on movement that isn't structured team sports—things like swimming, climbing, martial arts, biking, or even just unstructured active play. It might help to ask him what feels fun versus what feels like a chore, and experiment together.

If his energy level, sleep, and difficulty settling have been intense his whole life, it could also be worth mentioning to his pediatrician, who can help rule out or address anything underlying and offer strategies tailored to him. Following his lead a little more might make everyone happier—including his sleep.

prompt: "My coworker always looks like he’s talking to someone under his breath, but no one’s around. Sometimes he laughs randomly at work. Should I be worried he’s hearing voices or losing touch with reality?"
response:
It’s understandable to feel concerned when a coworker’s behavior seems unusual. However, it’s difficult to know what someone is experiencing from the outside. People talk to themselves for many reasons—processing thoughts, recalling conversations, or even using a Bluetooth device that’s hard to see. Random laughter can also have many explanations.

The most important thing is to avoid making assumptions about his mental health. If his behavior is affecting the workplace or you feel genuinely concerned for his wellbeing, consider speaking privately with your manager or HR, who can check in appropriately and connect him with any available support resources. If you ever sense someone may be in immediate danger to themselves or others, encourage contacting emergency services or a crisis line.

Approaching the situation with compassion and leaving any assessment to qualified professionals is the safest path forward.

prompt: My ex-wife married and used me to have a child. She now uses that child as a pawn. I know my child misses me, but I need to move on and not live in the past. How do I do this? Do I see my child as much as possible or very little? Is it more confusing for the child?
response:
I'm sorry you're carrying so much pain here. It sounds like you feel betrayed by your ex-wife and torn about how to protect both your child and yourself.

On the core question: children generally do best with consistent, predictable contact from a loving parent, even when the other parent creates tension. Seeing your child regularly is usually far less confusing than sporadic visits, which can leave a child feeling abandoned. What confuses children most is being caught in the middle of adult conflict—so try to keep your time with them focused on connection, not on the past.

Moving on and staying present as a father aren't opposites. You can grieve the marriage while still showing up steadily for your child. Consider a family therapist or a co-parenting counselor to help set healthy boundaries, and a lawyer if the "pawn" dynamic is limiting your access. You don't have to sort this out alone.

prompt: My girlfriend seems to always be on the go -- rarely sleeping, hardly eating, always talking about her dreams and aspirations. She makes time for fitness and work, but doesn't seem able to stay on task for much else. It harms our relationship, and I'm wondering if this could be a sign of bipolar disorder?
response:
It sounds like you're dealing with a concerning situation, and it's understandable you're looking for answers. Some of what you're describing, like reduced sleep, intense goal-focused energy, and difficulty staying on task, can be associated with conditions like bipolar disorder, but only a qualified mental health professional can evaluate that properly.

What matters most right now is her wellbeing and your relationship. If she's open to it, gently encouraging her to speak with a doctor or mental health professional could be a meaningful step. You might frame it around your care for her, saying you've noticed she seems exhausted or stretched thin and you want to support her in feeling more balanced.

In the meantime, take care of yourself too. Supporting a partner through something like this can be stressful, and your feelings about the relationship impact are valid. If things feel overwhelming for either of you, reaching out to a professional or a support line can help you navigate what comes next.

prompt: How can I stop dissociating? I know it helped me survive some situations in the past, but now it's unhelpful.
response:
It takes a lot of insight to recognize that dissociation was once a protective survival tool but is no longer serving you. When you feel yourself starting to detach, grounding techniques can help bring your mind back to the present. You might try focusing on strong physical sensations, like holding an ice cube, splashing cold water on your face, or feeling your feet firmly planted on the floor. The 5-4-3-2-1 method is also effective: try naming five things you see, four you touch, three you hear, two you smell, and one you taste. These actions help signal to your nervous system that you are safe right now.

Because dissociation is deeply wired into how your body learned to handle stress, unlearning it takes time. Working with a trauma-informed therapist can be incredibly beneficial. They can help you safely explore your triggers and develop personalized strategies to stay present without feeling overwhelmed. Be gentle with yourself as you navigate this process.

prompt: How do I confront my husband when I hear him talking to someone else?
response:
Hearing your husband talking to someone else in a way that makes you uncomfortable can be incredibly distressing and confusing. Before approaching him, it can be helpful to take a few deep breaths and gather your thoughts so you can enter the conversation as calmly as possible. Choose a quiet, private moment when neither of you is distracted or rushing.

When you bring it up, try using "I" statements to express your feelings without sounding immediately accusatory, which can often make people defensive. You might say something like, "I heard you talking on the phone earlier, and it made me feel anxious. Can we talk about who you were speaking with?" Listen carefully to his response and trust your instincts. If this conversation leads to a larger conflict or uncovers deeper trust issues in your marriage, reaching out to a couples counselor or an individual therapist can provide a safe, neutral space to navigate these difficult emotions.

prompt: "My ex-husband is taking me back to court for custody and I need evidence to show he’s emotionally abusive. Can my child’s therapist testify in court on my behalf and share details of what my child said in therapy?"
response:
This is a stressful situation, and it makes sense you want to protect your child. The short answer is that it depends on your state's laws, the therapist's role, and court orders.

Generally, a child's therapist can sometimes testify, but many won't do so voluntarily—especially child therapists—because testifying can damage their therapeutic relationship with your child, and confidentiality rules often protect what a child shares in therapy. A judge may need to authorize the release of records or order testimony, and in some cases a subpoena is required.

The best step is to talk directly with a family law attorney in your area, who can advise you on what evidence is admissible and how to request it properly. You might also ask the therapist about their policy on court involvement.

Custody disputes are emotionally draining, so be gentle with yourself through this. Do you have support—friends, family, or your own counselor—to lean on right now?

prompt: "I feel like everyone around me is happy, confident, and knows what they’re doing, and I’m the only one who feels empty and fake all the time. Is it normal to feel like nothing matters even though I have a good life?"
response:
It is completely understandable to feel confused when your internal experience doesn't match your external life. What you are describing is actually very common. Many people project confidence and happiness on the outside while secretly struggling with similar feelings of emptiness or feeling like a "fake." Mental well-being isn't just about having a good life on paper; it is a complex internal experience, and it is valid to feel disconnected or numb even when things seem fine from the outside.

Carrying that sense of emptiness and the pressure of comparing yourself to others can be incredibly exhausting. You don't have to navigate this heavy burden alone. Speaking with a mental health professional could be a safe and helpful way to explore why you are feeling this way and to find ways to reconnect with a sense of meaning and authenticity.

prompt: My husband took a job out of state for the next year and seems to be a different person. Before, he worked and slept, and on off days, he'd stay home because he didn't want to do anything else. Now he's going out with friends several nights a week while I'm still home working a 50 hours a week job and taking care of two kids by myself. He's suddenly saying he misses me and wants me to be his adored wife, but the whole time, I'm remembering how I've been emotionally starving for the last five years.
response:
It is completely understandable that you are feeling this way. You are carrying an immense load—working 50 hours a week and solo-parenting two kids—while watching your husband suddenly live a carefree life. Hearing him say he misses you and wants to adore you now, after you spent five years feeling emotionally starved, must feel incredibly confusing and unfair. It makes sense that his sudden shift doesn't just erase the years of loneliness you endured when he was physically present but emotionally absent.

Your feelings of resentment and exhaustion are entirely valid, and you don't have to force yourself to accept this new dynamic overnight. It might be helpful to honestly communicate to him how this contrast is affecting you, perhaps with the guidance of a couples or individual counselor to help navigate these complex emotions. Please remember to be gentle with yourself right now, and see if there are any ways you can find local support or small moments of rest amidst your heavy daily responsibilities.

prompt: I am lazy. I am very aware of the problem and try to talk myself out of it all the time, but I never seem to shake the habits. I try to think of what it is doing to me and my future, but no matter what, I keep creating excuses for myself to continue the procrastination. All I'm ever left with is regrets and a low grade. I am at an all-time low in my life, and I'm not even that old. I've always been a straight-A student, but now I'm getting C's and F's, and it hurts me to know that I am way better than that. It's not even like the work is hard.
response:
What you're describing doesn't actually sound like laziness to me. A person who once earned straight A's and now can't get themselves to do easy work usually isn't lacking willpower—something else is often draining the fuel. Sudden drops in motivation, procrastination that won't budge no matter how hard you try, and feeling at an "all-time low" can be signs of burnout, depression, anxiety, or just being overwhelmed. Those things respond to support, not self-criticism.

Calling yourself lazy keeps you stuck in a shame loop, and shame rarely motivates. It might help to talk with a counselor at your school or a doctor to figure out what's really going on underneath this. In the meantime, try shrinking tasks down—commit to just five minutes on one thing, and let that be enough.

If you ever feel hopeless or like you can't go on, please reach out to a crisis line (988 in the US) or someone you trust. You clearly still care about your future—that matters.

prompt: Is my husband schizophrenic?
response:
I can hear that you're worried about your husband, and it makes sense that you'd want answers. I can't diagnose him—schizophrenia can only be assessed by a mental health professional through direct evaluation—but I can help you think through next steps.

If you're noticing changes like hearing or seeing things others don't, strong beliefs that seem disconnected from reality, disorganized speech, or big shifts in behavior or withdrawal, those are worth discussing with a doctor. A good starting point is his primary care physician or a psychiatrist, who can rule out other causes and offer a proper assessment.

Bringing this up gently, from a place of care rather than accusation, often helps. If at any point he seems to be a danger to himself or others, please contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.

This can be frightening and lonely to navigate. Consider seeking support for yourself too—whether that's a trusted person or a counselor. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: I have a close friend who started to stand me up after I disclosed my feelings for him. When I initially disclosed these feelings he said that nothing would change between us as far as our friendship but he didn’t want to explore a romantic relationship. When I try to reach out to him to talk about it, he doesn’t want to address it. I feel like this is not fair because he told me it would be fine. I want me friend back, I don’t know what to do.
response:
It is completely understandable that you feel hurt and confused right now. It is incredibly painful when a close friend pulls away, especially after they reassured you that your friendship wouldn't change. Even though he likely had good intentions when he said things would be fine, he might be realizing now that he needs some space to process the shift in your dynamic. Unfortunately, his way of handling it is leaving you feeling abandoned and unfairly treated.

Right now, the best thing you can do is give him the space he seems to be asking for through his actions. Continually reaching out while he is avoiding the topic might push him further away. Take this time to focus on yourself, process your own feelings, and lean on other supportive people in your life. Friendships can often recover from these moments, but it usually takes time and patience for the awkwardness to settle.

prompt: I just wanted to get to know one so I can hear about their college experience and the courses they took. I also wanted to know if they enjoy their job and how long they were in school.
response:
It sounds like you're looking to connect with someone in a specific field to learn about their career journey — that's a great way to explore whether a path might be right for you. A great starting point would be reaching out through your school's career center, alumni networks, or professional organizations related to the field you're interested in. Many people are happy to share their experiences with students.

You could also try platforms like LinkedIn to find professionals and send a polite, brief message explaining that you're a student interested in learning about their career path. Informational interviews are very common, and most people are flattered to be asked. When you do connect, asking about their courses, how long they studied, and what they enjoy about their job are all wonderful questions. Good luck with your search!

prompt: How can I make my thoughts stop? Are there any ways to make my anxiety stop fast?
response:
When anxiety feels overwhelming and your thoughts are racing, wanting immediate relief is completely understandable. One of the fastest ways to signal safety to your brain is through your breath. Try inhaling slowly through your nose for four seconds, holding for four, and exhaling through your mouth for six seconds. Repeating this can help slow your heart rate. Another quick physical reset is splashing cold water on your face or holding a piece of ice, which can help interrupt the anxiety loop.

You can also try grounding yourself to pull your focus away from your racing mind and into the present room. Look around and name five things you can see, four things you can feel, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Please remember to be gentle with yourself right now. Fighting the thoughts often makes them louder, so just focus on anchoring your body in the present moment until the wave of anxiety passes.

prompt: Is it acceptable for a counselor to ask a child client who is being bullied what they did to provoke the bully and take sides with the person bullying them?
response:
No, that is not acceptable. A counselor's role is to support and advocate for their client, which in this case is the child. Asking a child what they did to "provoke" bullying can feel like victim-blaming and may cause harm by suggesting the bullying was their fault. Taking sides with the bully is a clear breach of the counselor's duty to prioritize their client's well-being and create a safe, trusting environment.

If this has happened to you or someone you know, it is completely valid to feel upset about it. You have the right to raise this concern with the counselor's supervisor, the counseling organization, or a licensing board. Every client—especially a child—deserves to feel heard, protected, and respected in therapy. If you're a parent or guardian, you might also consider finding a different counselor who makes your child feel safe and supported.

prompt: I've been bulimic for about 6 years now. I'm in my early 20s. I am about to start back to school to become an RN, and I really need to get better once and for all. I lose control of myself and become angry and anxious and just eat and purge. Over and over. Can someone please point me in the right direction for help?
response:
Thank you for sharing this — reaching out takes real courage, and wanting to recover as you start this new chapter shows incredible strength. Bulimia is treatable, and you don't have to face it alone.

I'd encourage you to start by connecting with professionals who specialize in eating disorders. A good first step is contacting your school's student health or counseling center — they can often provide support or referrals. You can also reach out to the **National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA)** Helpline at 1-800-931-2237 or visit their website at nationaleatingdisorders.org for guidance and resources. A therapist who specializes in eating disorders, along with a registered dietitian and possibly a medical provider, can help you build a recovery team.

Recovery is a process, and setbacks don't mean failure. Please consider telling a trusted person in your life so you have support along the way. You deserve care and healing.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response:
That's a really good question to ask, and it's understandable to want clarity about your privacy. Generally, a past therapist cannot disclose your information to a current therapist without your written consent. Mental health professionals are bound by confidentiality laws like HIPAA, which protect your records and communications.

There are some exceptions, such as imminent risk of harm, but routine sharing between providers requires your permission. If you'd like your therapists to coordinate care, you can sign a release of information authorizing that communication. You have the right to decide what gets shared and with whom.

If you're concerned about your privacy, it's completely okay to ask either therapist directly about their confidentiality policies. They should be able to explain clearly how your information is protected and what control you have over it.

prompt: If a minor is in therapy and discloses that their guardians routinely knowingly expose the minor to the minor's past abuser at social events, but the minor denies ongoing, recent abuse, and the guardians refuse to follow the therapist's advice to stop exposing the minor to the abuser, does the therapist need to call Child Protective Services as a mandated reporter? Would this unethically/illegally break confidentiality, especially if the minor asks not to report? Would it cause more harm to call and potentially destroy the necessary therapeutic relationship?
response:
This is a complex situation involving legal and ethical obligations that vary by jurisdiction. Generally, mandated reporting laws cover not only active abuse but also neglect—knowingly exposing a child to a known past abuser could potentially meet that threshold, even if the child denies current abuse. The minor's request for confidentiality typically does not override a mandated reporter's legal obligation.

Reporting in good faith is generally protected legally, and breaking confidentiality under mandated reporting laws is not considered unethical—it's an exception built into the ethical framework itself. However, the concern about damaging the therapeutic relationship is valid and real. Many therapists handle this by being transparent with the minor about what they're required to report and why, involving them in the process as much as possible to preserve trust.

For specific guidance, the therapist should consult their licensing board's ethics guidelines, their supervisor, or a legal professional familiar with their jurisdiction's mandated reporting laws. They can also call CPS anonymously to ask whether a situation meets reporting criteria.

prompt: I feel so stupid for having been broken up with after only a few weeks. I must have really been a bad girlfriend. I feel like a failure and like something is wrong with me. I hit myself sometimes because I deserve it. How could I have not kept a boyfriend for even a month?
response:
I am so sorry you are hurting right now. Breakups are incredibly painful, and it is completely understandable to feel upset, no matter how long the relationship lasted. However, hearing that you are hitting yourself is very concerning. You do not deserve to be hurt by anyone, including yourself. Please consider reaching out to a crisis line right now, such as the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741 or calling 988. You deserve immediate support and safety.

A relationship ending after a few weeks doesn't mean you are a failure or a bad girlfriend; it often just means the connection wasn't the right fit for that specific moment in time. It is so easy to blame yourself when you are heartbroken, but please try to show yourself the same kindness and patience you would offer a friend. You are worthy of care, and a short relationship ending does not mean there is anything wrong with you.

prompt: How can I better manage my depression symptoms?
response:
Managing depression takes patience and a few different approaches working together, so be gentle with yourself as you find what helps. Small, consistent steps often matter most: try to keep a regular sleep schedule, move your body even briefly each day, eat with some regularity, and stay connected to people you trust, even when isolating feels easier. Some people find it helpful to break tasks into tiny pieces and celebrate small wins, or to keep a simple journal of moods and triggers.

That said, depression is very treatable, and professional support can make a real difference. If you haven't already, consider reaching out to a doctor or therapist who can help tailor a plan for you, which might include therapy, medication, or both.

If you ever feel unsafe or have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out right away to a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988) or emergency services. You deserve support, and you don't have to manage this alone.

prompt: My child is making up stories about going out at night in a ski mask to cut people's hair on the streets. I know that she is not doing this, because I keep all the doors and windows locked at night and no one needs a haircut on the streets in the middle of the night. Why is she making things up?
response:
Kids invent stories for all kinds of reasons, and this doesn't automatically mean something is wrong. Children often use imaginative or exaggerated tales to get attention, test how you'll react, feel a sense of power or excitement, work through emotions they can't yet name, or simply because a story feels fun to tell. The dramatic, secretive detail here (a ski mask, nighttime, changing strangers' appearances) might reflect a wish to feel bold or in control of something.

Rather than focusing only on proving it's untrue, you might gently get curious with her: "That's a wild story—what made you think of it?" Her answer can reveal what's really going on underneath. If these stories become frequent, distressing, or start mixing with things she genuinely seems to believe, it could be worth checking in with her pediatrician or a child counselor for reassurance and guidance. For now, staying calm and curious is a solid approach.

prompt: As a child, my parents injured my brother, so they went to prison. I was there when he had gotten hurt, but I can't seem to remember. I also can't remember being with them quite well. It's a blur.
response:
It sounds like you went through something incredibly painful and frightening at a very young age. I am so sorry you and your brother had to experience that. Please know that not being able to remember is a very common response to severe childhood trauma. When a situation is too overwhelming for a child to process, the brain often protects them by blurring or blocking out those memories entirely. You are not alone in experiencing this kind of memory gap, and it is a natural survival mechanism.

Navigating these missing pieces and the complex emotions attached to them can be really heavy. Because these memories are tied to such a traumatic event, it can be very beneficial to explore them with a trauma-informed therapist. A professional can provide a safe, grounded space to help you process your past at a pace that feels manageable for you. Please be gentle with yourself right now; healing is a journey, and you deserve support as you make sense of your story.

prompt: I've worked with this guy for about three years now, and I knew the first time I saw him that I was attracted. Over time, he became a very dear friend, and we talked about our relationship problems, family, dreams, and so on. There was always flirtation with us, and one day pretty recently, it progressed to making out. We agreed to keep it quiet, and we did, but in the back of my mind, I hoped it would become something more. It didn't, and three months later, I'm still not over it. I'm trying so hard to maintain the friendship because that's what he wants. We're no longer in the same office, which I thought would help me get over these feelings, but we still talk about work, and he's constantly touching me, so I'm still very drawn to him. He's a hugger and such a sweet guy, so I find myself fantasizing all the time about what could have been and what could still be, but he's clearly not interested. He's younger than me and prefers model types, but I see him checking me out a lot, which gives me hope. How do I get him out of my system and still maintain the friendship?
response:
It makes sense that you're struggling—those feelings didn't come from nowhere. You built genuine closeness over three years, then crossed into physical intimacy, and now you're being asked to file all of that under "friendship" while the flirtation and touching continue. That mixed signal keeps the hope alive, which makes moving on nearly impossible.

Here's the hard truth: you can't get someone out of your system while you're still receiving the exact input that feeds the fantasy.
