I think I just need to rest up a bit and then go full force getting a second or even a third opinion. There's got to be some experimental treatment out there that would take me on as a test subject. How could you help me muster up the courage and determination to forge on?
response:
Facing a Stage IV diagnosis and hearing an unfamiliar term like palliative care can feel overwhelming, and it makes sense that you're searching for hope and a path forward. Wanting to pursue second and third opinions, and to explore clinical trials, is a completely reasonable and empowered choice—many people do exactly that, and seeking more information doesn't mean giving up.

One thing worth knowing: palliative care isn't only end-of-life care. It focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life, and it can run alongside active or experimental treatment. Asking your oncologist to clarify that distinction might ease some of the fear.

For finding trials, resources like ClinicalTrials.gov or major cancer centers can be a starting point, and academic hospitals often take referrals. Bringing a trusted person to appointments can help you stay grounded.

Resting first is wise—determination is easier when you're not depleted. And if the heaviness feels too big to carry alone, please reach out to your care team or a counselor. You deserve support in this.

prompt: Lately I have been feeling very fatigued, my hair is falling out, I have gained weight and some more concerning symptoms. My husband says it’s most likely my depression and although that might be somewhat true I think something else is going on. Every time I tell him that I think it’s more than depression, he tells me I wrong. Is he gaslighting me?
response:
It sounds really frustrating to feel dismissed when you're worried about your own body. First, on the medical side: fatigue, hair loss, and weight gain can absolutely have physical causes—thyroid issues, hormonal imbalances, anemia, and other conditions can cause exactly these symptoms and are worth checking out. Trusting your instinct that "something else is going on" is reasonable, and the clearest next step is to see a doctor for bloodwork and an evaluation. You don't need anyone's permission to seek that.

As for gaslighting—it's hard to know intent from a few interactions. Sometimes people minimize out of their own anxiety or a genuine (if misguided) belief they're reassuring you. But whether or not it's intentional, the effect on you matters: feeling repeatedly unheard about your health is real, and you deserve to be taken seriously.

Consider making that appointment for yourself, and if it helps, bring a written list of your symptoms so your concerns are documented. You know your body.

prompt: "I was recently diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, and nothing I’m doing seems to work. Should I ask my doctor for Xanax or something stronger?"
response:
It makes sense to feel frustrated when things aren't improving—managing anxiety can be a real struggle, and reaching for relief is understandable.

Bringing this up with your doctor is absolutely the right move, and it's worth having an open conversation rather than requesting a specific medication. Benzodiazepines like Xanax can help in some situations, but they're usually used short-term because of concerns like tolerance and dependence, so many providers start with other options for ongoing anxiety. What might help most is telling your doctor exactly what you've tried, how it's going, and how anxiety is affecting your daily life—that lets them tailor a plan for you, which may include different medications, therapy like CBT, or a combination. If you're already on a medication that isn't working, mention that too, since dosages and options can be adjusted.

You deserve treatment that actually helps, and it's okay to keep advocating for yourself until you find it.

prompt: I heard a rumor that I may be fired soon and I'm a wreck over it. Some colleagues say I may have a chance to do better and stay, but I feel so low and depressed over even the thought of them considering firing me. I've been having troubles in my relationship. Do I just have to accept that at work they don't care about my personal issues and leave if they ask me to?
response:
It is completely understandable that you are feeling overwhelmed and low right now. Dealing with relationship troubles is exhausting on its own, and adding the stress of a rumor about losing your job is a heavy burden to carry. It makes sense that you feel hurt at the thought of being let go, especially when you are already going through a hard time personally.

While it can be a harsh reality that many workplaces focus primarily on professional performance rather than personal struggles, that doesn't mean your well-being isn't important. Since your colleagues mentioned there might be a chance to improve and stay, it might help to have an open, proactive conversation with your manager to clarify expectations rather than waiting in fear. Please remember to be gentle with yourself right now. Navigating both personal and professional stress at the same time is incredibly difficult, and it is okay to seek support from a counselor or trusted friend to help you through this heavy season.

prompt: Most days are good but sometimes, clear out of the blue, that knife-point robbery just pops into my head. How can I put that in the past once and for all?
response:
What you're describing—an unwanted memory of a traumatic event surfacing without warning—is a very common response to something as frightening as being robbed at knife-point. Your mind is still processing what happened, and these intrusions don't mean you're doing anything wrong or failing to "get over it."

The goal isn't always to erase the memory completely, but to reduce its intensity so it no longer catches you off guard. When it pops up, try grounding yourself in the present: notice five things you can see, take slow breaths, and remind yourself that you're safe now. If these moments are frequent or distressing, a therapist trained in trauma approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused CBT can be genuinely effective at helping the memory lose its grip.

Consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can work with you directly. You've survived something terrifying, and wanting relief is completely understandable—healing is possible.

prompt: Is it acceptable for a counselor to ask a child client who is being bullied what they did to provoke the bully and take sides with the person bullying them?
response:
No, that's not acceptable. A counselor asking a bullied child what they did to "provoke" it, or taking the bully's side, places blame on the victim and can deepen their hurt and shame. Bullying is never the target's fault, and a good counselor should help the child feel safe, heard, and supported—not interrogated or judged.

If this is happening to a child you care about, it's worth taking seriously. Consider raising your concerns with the school, requesting a different counselor, or seeking support elsewhere. You might also ask the child gently how their sessions feel to them.

If the child seems significantly distressed, withdrawn, or is talking about harming themselves, please reach out to a trusted professional or a crisis line right away. Trusting your instincts here is reasonable—kids deserve counselors who protect and advocate for them.

prompt: It's really hard to not have negative feelings about friends who don't put any effort into nourishing our relationship.
response:
It's completely valid to feel hurt and frustrated when friendships feel one-sided. You're investing care and energy, and it's painful when that isn't reciprocated. Those feelings don't make you a bad friend — they show you value connection deeply.

It might help to remember that people's capacity often shifts due to their own life circumstances, stress, or mental health, and their lack of effort may not be about you personally. That said, it's also okay to reassess where you place your energy. You deserve relationships that feel mutual and fulfilling. Consider gently expressing how you feel to friends you value — sometimes people genuinely don't realize. And if certain connections remain draining despite your efforts, it's okay to step back and make space for people who can meet you halfway.

prompt: How do I overcome being jealous of my boyfriends mother?
response:
Feeling jealous of your boyfriend's mother is more common than you might think, and it doesn't make you a bad person. These feelings often stem from a fear of being replaced or not feeling like a priority. It's worth reflecting on what specifically triggers the jealousy, whether it's time spent together, inside jokes, or something else.

Consider having an open, gentle conversation with your boyfriend about your feelings, focusing on what you need from the relationship rather than criticizing his relationship with his mom. Remember that a strong maternal bond doesn't diminish what you bring to his life. Working on your own self-worth and recognizing that different relationships fulfill different needs can also help. If these feelings are causing significant distress, speaking with a counselor could provide you with personalized strategies to work through them.

prompt: I had a panic attack at a friend's birthday party. Instead of her or anyone trying to help, my friend instead recorded a video and posted it on TikTok and now my panic attack has gone viral. Should I ghost my friend? Should I give her the benefit of the doubt and allow some time for her to apologize and give an explanation?
response:
I am so incredibly sorry you experienced this. Having a panic attack is already a deeply vulnerable and frightening experience, and having it recorded and shared without your consent is a massive breach of trust and privacy. It is completely understandable that you are feeling hurt, humiliated, and questioning this friendship.

You do not owe her the benefit of the doubt, especially when her actions caused you public distress instead of offering support. Whether you choose to step away completely or wait for an explanation is entirely up to what feels safest for you right now. If you haven't already, you have every right to demand she take the video down immediately, or you can report the video to the platform yourself. Please prioritize your own emotional well-being right now, and remember that you deserve to surround yourself with people who respect your boundaries and offer genuine care when you need it most.

prompt: How can I control my anxiety when I have Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
response:
Managing anxiety with OCD can feel exhausting, and it makes sense that you're looking for ways to cope. One of the most effective approaches for OCD is a form of therapy called Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), which gently helps you face anxious thoughts without giving in to compulsions. Over time, this can reduce the grip anxiety has on you. If you're not already working with a mental health professional, connecting with one who specializes in OCD can make a real difference.

In the moment, grounding techniques may help—slow breathing, naming things you can see and hear, or reminding yourself that anxious thoughts are not facts and don't require action. Being patient and compassionate with yourself matters too; setbacks are part of the process, not failures.

If your anxiety ever feels overwhelming or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You don't have to manage this alone, and support is available.

prompt: I am a teacher who sees one of your clients. I am worried that they are experiencing anxiety all the time and seem to have a low distress tolerance threshold. I think you should talk to her mom about getting medication.
response:
It sounds like you genuinely care about this student and are noticing real signs of distress—that kind of attentiveness makes a meaningful difference for young people.

I'm an AI assistant, so I'm not able to see clients, share information, or coordinate care with anyone. But your observations are valuable, and there are people who can act on them. If you have a school counselor, psychologist, or nurse, sharing what you've noticed with them is a strong next step, as they can involve the family appropriately and connect the student with an evaluation. Decisions about medication would come from a medical or mental health provider after assessing her directly, so encouraging a professional evaluation—rather than a specific treatment—tends to be the most helpful framing.

If she ever seems to be in immediate danger or crisis, please follow your school's emergency protocol right away. Thank you for looking out for her.

prompt: We've been in a long distance relationship for two and a half years. I recently saw his phone and saw the people he texts the most and one of them was a female coworker. I don't know how to approach this situation. How do I ask him about it?.
response:
It's understandable to feel uneasy, especially in a long-distance relationship where trust is so important. When approaching him, try to choose a calm moment and use "I" statements to express your feelings without sounding accusatory. For example, you might say, "I noticed you've been texting a coworker frequently, and I'm feeling a bit insecure about it. Can we talk about your relationship with her?"

Being open about your feelings rather than making assumptions gives him the opportunity to reassure you and explain the context. A healthy partner will understand your concern and be willing to have an honest conversation. Pay attention to how he responds—whether he's patient and transparent or dismissive and defensive can tell you a lot. Long-distance relationships require extra communication and trust, so it's important that you feel comfortable expressing your needs. If the conversation leaves you feeling more anxious or unheard, that's worth reflecting on as well.

prompt: How involved should my partner be in my counseling process? Do you think it would help with keeping our marriage together?
response:
That's a thoughtful question, and the answer really depends on what you're working through in counseling and what you both want from the process.

If your goals are personal—like managing your own stress, healing from past experiences, or building coping skills—individual counseling with occasional partner check-ins can be valuable. If the concerns center on your relationship itself, couples counseling may be a better fit, where you both attend together and work as a team. Many people actually do both.

Involving your partner can strengthen a marriage when there's mutual willingness, openness, and respect for each other's pace. It's worth having an honest conversation with them about what they'd feel comfortable with, and discussing it with your counselor, who can help tailor the right approach for your situation.

Counseling can be a meaningful support, though no single tool guarantees an outcome. What matters most is that you're both invested in growing together.

prompt: How can I make my thoughts stop? Are there any ways to make my anxiety stop fast?
response:
When anxious thoughts spiral, a few quick tools can help calm your body in the moment. Try slow breathing—inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 6—since a longer exhale signals your nervous system to settle. Grounding also works well: name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, and 1 you taste. Splashing cold water on your face or holding something cold can also interrupt the intensity fast.

Racing thoughts are hard to stop directly, but you can loosen their grip by not fighting them—let them pass like background noise rather than treating each one as urgent. Writing them down can help get them out of your head, too.

If anxiety is happening often or feeling overwhelming, talking with a doctor or therapist can make a real difference. And if you ever feel unsafe or in crisis, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You deserve support with this.

prompt: I have found myself struggling in grad school to focus on the difficult workload. I have always been a high achiever in school and people expect great things from me. I have always been told that I am a brilliant student and learner and my work is always done with such attention to detail, but personally I feel like it takes me twice as long as other students to complete any work. When my friends might be finished with their work and having fun I would often only be halfway done. What can I do to work on my attention?
response:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of pressure, and it's completely understandable that grad school's demands feel overwhelming. The gap between others' expectations and your own experience can be exhausting, especially when you're working hard but feeling like it's never enough.

A few things might help: First, consider breaking tasks into smaller, timed intervals (like 25-minute focused sessions with short breaks) to make starting feel less daunting. Second, try to limit comparisons—many students hide their struggles, so you may not be as far behind as you think. Third, if focus difficulties are significantly impacting your daily life, it could be worth talking to a campus counselor or healthcare provider who can offer personalized support and explore whether something deeper is affecting your concentration. You deserve support that meets your actual needs, not just the expectations others have placed on you.

prompt: Is my husband schizophrenic?
response:
It sounds like you are going through a stressful time, and it is completely understandable to be concerned about your husband's well-being. However, as an AI, I cannot diagnose mental health conditions like schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is a complex disorder that requires a thorough evaluation by a qualified psychiatrist or medical professional to accurately identify.

If you are noticing concerning changes in his behavior, thoughts, or perception of reality, the best step is to gently encourage him to see a doctor. If he is hesitant, you might consider reaching out to a mental health professional or a local support organization yourself to get guidance on how to help him and how to support your own well-being during this difficult time. If you ever feel that he is in a crisis or poses an immediate danger to himself or others, please contact emergency services right away.

prompt: Everyone around me is much smarter and flaunts it. Everyone around me is skinny, and here I am trying to throw up so I'm not fat. Everything I do is wrong, and I can't seem to do anything right! No one else at school seems to feel the way I do! Is this normal teenage girls feelings? I don't think these feelings are normal.
response:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this much pain. What you're describing — feeling like everyone else is smarter, thinner, better — and the urge to throw up to control your body, those feelings are heavy and exhausting. While many teens struggle with comparison and self-doubt, throwing up to try to change your body is harmful and is something worth talking about with a trusted adult or health professional who can support you.

You don't have to figure this out alone. Please consider reaching out to someone you trust — a parent, school counselor, doctor, or a helpline. In the US, you can text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor, or call the National Eating Disorders Association helpline at 1-800-931-2237. You deserve real support and care, not to suffer in silence. What you're feeling matters, and help is available.

prompt: I had a panic attack at a friend's birthday party. Instead of her or anyone trying to help, my friend instead recorded a video and posted it on TikTok and now my panic attack has gone viral. Should I ghost my friend? Should I give her the benefit of the doubt and allow some time for her to apologize and give an explanation?
response:
I'm really sorry this happened. A panic attack is a vulnerable, frightening moment, and having it recorded and shared without your consent is a genuine betrayal of trust. Your hurt and anger make complete sense.

You don't have to decide everything right now. It's fair to ask her directly why she did that and whether she'll take the video down—her response will tell you a lot about whether this friendship is safe for you. Giving someone a chance to explain isn't the same as excusing them; you can listen while still holding firm that what she did caused real harm. If she minimizes it or refuses to remove the video, stepping back is a reasonable way to protect yourself, and you don't owe anyone endless access to you.

You might also report the video to TikTok to have it removed. Whatever you choose about the friendship, please be gentle with yourself—you deserve people who help you, not film you.

prompt: I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.
response:
I'm so sorry you experienced this. Crying is a completely normal human response to stress, and feeling emotional at a new job—especially your first one—doesn't make you weak or unprofessional. What you went through sounds really overwhelming, and it's understandable that you're worried about how things stand now.

That said, no one should be pushed to tears at work, especially a teenager just starting out. If your boss's management style is making you feel this way, it might be worth talking to a trusted adult—a parent, guardian, teacher, or school counselor—who can help you think through your options. You deserve a workplace that treats you with respect, and if this environment isn't healthy for you, it's okay to consider whether it's the right fit. Your wellbeing matters far more than any job.

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response:
In most cases, a past therapist cannot share your information with a current therapist unless you give them explicit permission to do so. Mental health professionals are bound by strict privacy laws and ethical guidelines that protect your confidentiality. To share your records or discuss your treatment, they typically need you to sign a formal "Release of Information" document.

You have the right to decide what information is shared and with whom. If you want your new therapist to have your past records to help with your current care, you can authorize that transfer. However, if you prefer to keep your past treatment completely private, you are entirely within your rights to withhold that consent. The only rare exceptions to this rule involve situations where there is an immediate risk of severe harm to yourself or others, or a court order, where therapists may be legally required to share information to ensure safety.

prompt: I loved him more than anything. He passed away on our anniversary which was also the day I was going to apply for our apartment. I'm not handling it well. I moved to a new town and started a new life but nothing helps.
response:
I'm so deeply sorry for your loss. Losing someone you love that much, on a day that was meant to be celebratory, adds layers of pain that most people can't even begin to understand. The grief you're carrying is heavy, and it makes complete sense that starting fresh in a new town hasn't fixed it—grief doesn't respond to changes of scenery.

What you're experiencing isn't a failure to cope. It's the natural response to losing someone central to your life and your future. The apartment, the anniversary, the plans you had—those represent dreams that were interrupted, and mourning those dreams is just as real as mourning the person.

Please consider reaching out to a grief counselor or a local grief support group. You don't have to carry this alone, and talking with others who understand profound loss can help. You can also call or text 988 anytime if things become overwhelming. Your grief deserves support, and you deserve care as you navigate this.

prompt: I heard a rumor that I may be fired soon and I'm a wreck over it. Some colleagues say I may have a chance to do better and stay, but I feel so low and depressed over even the thought of them considering firing me. I've been having troubles in my relationship. Do I just have to accept that at work they don't care about my personal issues and leave if they ask me to?
response:
That sounds incredibly stressful—facing job uncertainty while your relationship is also struggling is a heavy load to carry at once. It makes complete sense that you feel low and shaken; anyone would.

A few things might help untangle this. Right now it's a rumor, not a decision, and your colleagues saying you have a chance to stay is worth holding onto. If it feels possible, a calm conversation with your manager about where you actually stand could replace the anxiety of guessing with real information. You don't necessarily have to accept the worst before it happens.

And no, you don't have to face this alone or just "leave if they ask." Try to separate what you can influence at work from what you can't, and lean on someone you trust for support. If the depression deepens or feels overwhelming, please consider reaching out to a counselor or your doctor. You deserve support through this, at work and personally.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response:
A good counselor draws on several core skills. Active listening is fundamental—giving full attention, reflecting back what's said, and noticing tone and body language, not just words. Empathy allows them to understand a person's experience without judgment, while genuine warmth and respect help build trust and rapport.

Strong communication matters too: asking open questions, summarizing, and knowing when to stay silent. Counselors also need self-awareness to recognize their own biases and reactions, along with clear professional boundaries and ethics. Patience, cultural sensitivity, and the ability to stay calm during difficult moments round out the picture, as does knowing their limits and when to refer someone to other support.

If you're exploring this because you're considering becoming a counselor, that's a meaningful path—many of these skills grow with training and practice. If you're asking because you're looking for support yourself, I'm glad to talk more about what you're hoping to find.

prompt: "How can I stop replaying fights with my parents in my head every day? I want to stop holding grudges and just move on, but I don’t know how."
response:
It's really exhausting to get stuck replaying those conversations, and it makes sense that you want to move forward. One helpful approach is to notice when the replay starts and gently redirect your attention to something in the present moment—what you're doing right now, something you can see or hear. You don't have to force the thoughts away; just acknowledge them and shift focus. Writing down what happened and what you felt can also help externalize the emotions so they feel less trapped in your head.

Moving on doesn't mean pretending things didn't hurt or that you agree with what happened. It can mean deciding that carrying this anger isn't serving you anymore. You might try reminding yourself that holding a grudge is keeping you connected to something painful, and you're allowed to set it down. If these thoughts are persistent and affecting your daily life, talking with a counselor or therapist could help you process the underlying feelings in a deeper way.

prompt: It's been almost a year since my ex-boyfriend broke up with me after he cheated on me many times. I had found out about a month before, but I hadn't told him I knew because I didn't want us to break up. I used to have very low self-esteem, and I think it might have to do with my dad being an alcoholic. My father cheated on my mother when I was little. I wonder if this pain has to do with that. My ex-boyfriend and I were only dating for five months, but I still can't get over this betrayal. I'm not sure what to feel to get over it: forgiveness? Hate? He helped me financially after our break up by lending me $3000, so I'm grateful for that. I still hate him for what he did and still want him to like me although we're not even talking anymore. We follow each other on Instagram and that's it. I feel like I still need his validation. This is haunting me day and night. I want to focus on my new relationship and goals, but I keep obsessing over this and keep checking my ex-boyfriend's Instagram and Facebook. I feel so bad and keep having nightmares.
response:
It is completely understandable that you are feeling so conflicted. Betrayal leaves a deep wound, and it makes sense that your ex's infidelity is bringing up painful echoes of your father's actions. When we experience childhood trauma, like a parent's betrayal, it can deeply affect our self-esteem and make us crave validation from the very people who hurt us. It is okay to feel a mix of gratitude for his financial help and anger for his betrayal; human emotions are rarely simple.

To help break this cycle and focus on your new relationship, you might want to consider unfollowing or muting him on social media. Constantly seeing his updates can keep the wound open and fuel the obsession. Healing doesn't necessarily require you to force feelings of forgiveness or hate; it is more about slowly redirecting your energy back to yourself. Since these feelings and nightmares are haunting you, speaking with a counselor could be incredibly helpful for unpacking these childhood patterns and rebuilding your self-esteem.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response:
Thank you for sharing this so clearly. The fact that you recognize the rage as disproportionate and separate from who you are shows real insight. That self-awareness, while painful, is actually important. Wanting to not be consumed by anger shows you're oriented toward healing.

Extreme anger that feels disproportionate can stem from many things: accumulated stress, past experiences, nervous system dysregulation, or other underlying factors. A therapist, particularly one who works with anger or emotion regulation, could help you understand what's driving the intensity and develop ways to work with it. You don't have to figure this out alone. If you ever feel your safety or someone else's is at risk, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away.

prompt: If a minor is in therapy and discloses that their guardians routinely knowingly expose the minor to the minor's past abuser at social events, but the minor denies ongoing, recent abuse, and the guardians refuse to follow the therapist's advice to stop exposing the minor to the abuser, does the therapist need to call Child Protective Services as a mandated reporter? Would this unethically/illegally break confidentiality, especially if the minor asks not to report? Would it cause more harm to call and potentially destroy the necessary therapeutic relationship?
response:
This is a very complex and painful situation. Mandated reporting laws vary by location, but generally, therapists are legally required to report situations where a minor is suspected of being abused, neglected, or placed in danger. In many jurisdictions, guardians knowingly exposing a child to a past abuser—despite professional warnings—can be considered a "failure to protect" or a form of neglect, which often triggers the legal duty to report to Child Protective Services (CPS).

Because mandated reporting is a legal requirement designed to protect vulnerable individuals, making a report is an established exception to confidentiality, meaning it is neither illegal nor unethical even if the minor asks not to report. While therapists care deeply about preserving the therapeutic relationship and avoiding additional distress for the minor, the legal and ethical obligation to ensure the child's safety must come first. If you are navigating this, consulting with a clinical supervisor, a legal professional, or a professional ethics board in your specific jurisdiction can provide definitive guidance.

prompt: How do I grow into a new person? What are some ways I can help myself?
response:
Wanting to grow into a new version of yourself is a meaningful and hopeful goal. Real change usually happens gradually, through small, consistent steps rather than a single dramatic shift. A good place to start is getting clear on what "new person" means to you—what values, habits, or feelings you want more of in your life. From there, you can pick one or two small actions to practice regularly, since repeated behavior tends to shape who we become over time.

Some things that help many people include journaling to notice patterns in your thoughts, setting realistic goals, building routines around sleep and movement, and surrounding yourself with people who support the direction you're heading. Be patient and kind with yourself along the way—growth includes setbacks, and those don't mean you're failing.

If you ever feel stuck or overwhelmed, talking with a counselor or therapist can give you personalized guidance. What area of your life feels most important to work on first?

prompt: I am an international student, and it is my first semester in graduate school in the United States. I faced a cultural shock, and I was so depressed when I arrived here. My counselor in the university was my savior. He helped me a great deal. Now I am going back to my country for a vacation. I was thinking to get him something special with my country's name on it, and I remembered that he likes wine. My country is known for that. Is it appropriate to give him wine as a gift after Christmas?
response:
It is wonderful to hear that you found such great support during your transition to graduate school and that your counselor was able to help you navigate your culture shock. Wanting to express your gratitude is a very kind and natural response.

However, in the United States, counselors and therapists are bound by strict professional and ethical guidelines regarding gifts. Accepting alcohol, or gifts of significant monetary value, is generally not permitted as it can blur professional boundaries. Instead of wine, the most meaningful and appropriate gift you could give is a heartfelt, handwritten card expressing how much his support has meant to you. If you still want to share a piece of your culture, a very small, inexpensive token—like a postcard from your country or a traditional snack—might be acceptable, but a sincere note of thanks is always the safest and most cherished option.

prompt: I have four children. One of them is in her 20s, and she cannot afford to go, nor can I pay for her. She went last year for two weeks by herself.
response:
It sounds incredibly stressful to want to help your daughter but feel limited by financial constraints. As a parent, it is completely natural to want to provide the care she needs, and it can be heartbreaking when the costs are out of reach. Please remember that you are doing your best with the resources you have, and this financial barrier is not a failure on your part.

Since she went for two weeks last year, she has already shown a willingness to seek support, which is a very positive sign. You might encourage her to look into community health centers, which often offer services on a sliding scale based on income, or explore free support groups that can provide coping strategies and a sense of community. Simply being there to offer your emotional support and a listening ear makes a significant difference while you both navigate these hurdles.

prompt: We’ve been together almost three years. We argue and he ends it by telling me he doesn’t love me. It's hurtful because I am all about resolving the problem, and he dwells on the issue even if I drop what he's done and just swallow my pride and say I am sorry. How can this be resolved? We have kids, and I don't want a broken family because we can't communicate.
response:
It is incredibly painful to hear your partner say he doesn't love you during arguments, especially when you are trying so hard to resolve the conflict and keep your family together. When one person tries to fix the issue and the other uses hurtful words to shut down the conversation, it creates an emotionally exhausting dynamic. Constantly swallowing your pride and apologizing just to keep the peace is not a sustainable way for you to live.

Because these communication patterns are often deeply ingrained, resolving them requires both partners to be willing to change. You might consider suggesting couples counseling. A neutral professional can help both of you learn healthier ways to communicate and manage disagreements without resorting to hurtful statements. If he is unwilling to go, individual therapy could still provide you with a safe space to navigate your boundaries, process your feelings, and decide what is healthiest for you and your children moving forward.

prompt: "My ex-husband is taking me back to court for custody and I need evidence to show he’s emotionally abusive. Can my child’s therapist testify in court on my behalf and share details of what my child said in therapy?"
response:
I understand how stressful custody battles can be, especially when you're trying to protect your child. Whether a child's therapist can testify depends on your jurisdiction's laws around therapist-client privilege and confidentiality. In many places, therapy records and communications are protected, and a therapist generally cannot share what a child said in sessions without a court order or specific legal exceptions. Some states have rules about when a child's statements may be admitted in custody disputes.

This is really a question for a family law attorney who can advise you on the rules in your area, help you understand what evidence might be admissible, and guide you through the process of requesting court orders if needed. They can also help you think through other forms of documentation that might support your case.

Please consider reaching out to a lawyer as soon as possible, and if you're feeling overwhelmed, a counselor or support line can help you cope with the stress of this situation. You don't have to navigate this alone.

prompt: My child has a history of severe trauma and has made suicidal statements throughout the years at school to get out of assignments and get attention from teachers. She is not suicidal and she has never said this to me at home. I think she's doing it for attention; does she need therapy?
response:
Any suicidal statements, even those that seem tied to avoiding tasks or seeking attention, should be taken seriously and assessed by a qualified mental health professional. A history of severe trauma is itself an important reason to consider therapy, as trauma can affect children in complex ways that aren't always visible at home. A therapist can help determine what's driving these statements and provide appropriate support.

It's also worth noting that "attention-seeking" behavior often signals an unmet need, and a professional can help identify what that need might be. Please consider reaching out to a licensed child therapist or psychologist for an evaluation, and if your child ever makes any statements suggesting immediate risk, contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.

prompt: If two parents are in a custody battle, is the counselor allowed to speak with both parents? Can the counselor write a letter or testify for court regarding which parent is better and who the child should be with?
response:
These are important questions, and the answers depend on the counselor's role and the laws where you live.

Generally, a child's treatment therapist should be cautious about taking sides in a custody dispute. Their job is to support the child, not to evaluate which parent is "better." Many ethical guidelines actually discourage a treating therapist from making custody recommendations, because that creates a conflict of interest with the therapeutic relationship. Speaking with both parents may be appropriate for gathering information, but that's different from recommending placement.

Formal custody recommendations usually come from a separate, court-appointed evaluator who is specifically hired for that purpose. A counselor can sometimes write a letter or testify about what they've observed, but often only with proper consent or a court order.

Since custody laws and ethics rules vary by state and country, I'd encourage you to ask the counselor directly about their role, and to consult a family law attorney for guidance specific to your situation.

prompt: How can I get therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder without any money or insurance?
response:
Seeking help for PTSD is a brave step, and it is completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when finances are a barrier. There are several avenues you can explore to find care without insurance. Many communities have federally funded health centers or local mental health clinics that offer services on a sliding scale based on your income, which can sometimes mean free care. You can also look into local university psychology departments; they often have training clinics where graduate students provide therapy at a very low cost under the supervision of licensed professionals.

Additionally, organizations like the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) or the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) have free helplines and online locators to help you find affordable local resources and free support groups. If you ever feel in crisis or overwhelmed, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988 for immediate, free support.

prompt: After three failed diets over the past year, I think it's finally time that I get on one of those new weight control prescriptions. I still go to the gym four times a week but I've gained 20 pounds over the winter. Should I just stick with talk therapy and my self-help efforts or do the new medications really help maintain a healthy weight for someone with my history?
response:
It sounds incredibly frustrating to put in so much effort at the gym and with your diet, only to feel like you aren't seeing the results you want. It is completely understandable that you are exploring new options after a difficult winter.

Because weight management involves both physical and emotional factors, talk therapy and medical support often work well together rather than being an either-or choice. Therapy is wonderful for exploring your relationship with food and the emotional toll of dieting. However, I cannot give medical advice or determine if a weight-loss medication is right for your specific history. The best step is to have an open conversation with your primary care doctor. They can evaluate your health, explain how these new prescriptions work, and help you decide if combining medical support with your ongoing therapy and gym routine is the safest and most effective path forward for you.

prompt: Is it acceptable for a counselor to ask a child client who is being bullied what they did to provoke the bully and take sides with the person bullying them?
response:
It is not acceptable for a counselor to take the side of a bully or ask a child what they did to provoke being bullied. A counselor's primary role is to provide a safe, supportive, and non-judgmental space for their client. Asking a child how they provoked bullying is a form of victim-blaming, which can deeply damage a child's self-esteem and destroy the trust necessary for effective therapy. No one deserves to be bullied, and a mental health professional should focus on validating the child's experience, helping them process their feelings, and supporting them in navigating the situation safely.

If a counselor is behaving this way, it is completely valid to be concerned. It may be in the child's best interest for a parent or guardian to address this directly with the counselor or the clinic's management. Finding a new therapist who uses a supportive, empathetic approach is often the best step to ensure the child gets the safe and validating care they deserve.

prompt: I keep on begging him to come back. I am so unhappy with him but am so scared of being a single parent to our son. I was abused as a little girl and that has made to be very abusive to men. What should I do...
response:
It takes real courage to share this, and the fact that you're reflecting on these patterns shows how much you care about yourself and your son. It's completely understandable to feel scared about the future, especially when past wounds are so deeply tied to how you relate to others now.

Healing from childhood abuse and breaking cycles of harmful behavior often requires support that goes beyond what anyone can do alone. A therapist or counselor can help you process those early experiences, understand how they shape your relationships now, and develop healthier ways of coping. You deserve that support, and your son deserves a mom who is healing and whole. Consider reaching out to a domestic violence or trauma-informed counseling service in your area, as they understand these complexities with compassion and without judgment. You're not alone in this, and asking "what should I do" is already an important first step.

prompt: I was in therapy once, 4 years ago for PTSD, It did nothing for me and I know it is not going to work again. But I need help. What do i do?
response:
I hear how frustrating that experience was, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel hesitant to try again. One thing worth knowing is that not all therapy—or therapists—are the same. Different approaches, like EMDR, somatic therapy, or trauma-focused CBT, work in very different ways, and finding the right fit can make a huge difference.

That said, therapy isn't the only path to healing. Support groups, both online and in person, can be powerful because you're connecting with others who truly understand. Mindfulness practices, journaling, and body-based approaches like yoga can also help regulate the nervous system in ways that complement or even replace traditional therapy.

What matters most is that you've recognized you need support—that takes real courage. Consider talking to your doctor about what you're going through, as they can help guide you toward options that might feel more workable for you. You deserve to find something that helps, and it's okay to be selective about what that looks like.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response:
I am so sorry you are dealing with this. It sounds incredibly exhausting to manage a racing mind, anxiety, and sleep issues, especially when medications have caused such painful side effects. Because your symptoms are tied to a head injury and you are having severe physical reactions to medication, it is very important to share these specific side effects with a neurologist or your primary doctor. They can help explore alternative, non-medication therapies like cognitive rehabilitation, specialized counseling, or biofeedback.

In the meantime, you might find some relief through gentle grounding techniques. Focusing on your breathing, such as inhaling deeply for four seconds and exhaling for six, can help signal your nervous system to slow down. You could also try restorative practices like listening to guided sleep meditations, using a weighted blanket, or doing progressive muscle relaxation to help ease your racing thoughts before bed. Please be gentle with yourself as you navigate this.

prompt: My four year old daughter has been struggling with her milestones for as long as I can remember. Potty training has been an absolute nightmare, she refuses to go and will even sit on the toilet crying for half an hour while refusing to "go" at all. In fact she's never once used the toilet correctly. She gestures at herself in the mirror, looking at herself is one of her favorite hobbies, but anytime one of us is looking at her it feels like she's looking through us instead of at us. We were hoping that a half day at preschool would be helpful for her to develop out of these issues but they seem to persist. What can we try next?
response:
It sounds like you've been working hard to support your daughter, and it's understandable to feel concerned when these challenges persist. Some of what you're describing—difficulty with potty training, limited eye contact, and looking "through" people rather than at them—can be part of a range of developmental differences that are best understood through a professional evaluation.

I'd encourage you to talk with her pediatrician about what you're observing. They can refer you to a developmental specialist or early intervention program, which can provide a thorough assessment and, if needed, tailored strategies and therapies. Early support can make a meaningful difference, and you don't need to wait for things to resolve on their own before seeking guidance.

In the meantime, try to keep interactions low-pressure—forcing potty time when she's distressed may increase her anxiety around it. Follow her interests, celebrate small wins, and be gentle with yourselves too. You're clearly advocating for her, and that matters a lot.

prompt: Everyone around me is much smarter and flaunts it. Everyone around me is skinny, and here I am trying to throw up so I'm not fat. Everything I do is wrong, and I can't seem to do anything right! No one else at school seems to feel the way I do! Is this normal teenage girls feelings? I don't think these feelings are normal.
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting and painful to feel like you don't measure up to the people around you. While many teenagers struggle with self-esteem and body image, what you are describing goes beyond typical teenage stress. Trying to throw up to lose weight is a sign that you are dealing with something very serious, and it can be dangerous to your health. You are right to trust your instincts that these feelings are not something you should just have to accept as normal.

You deserve to feel safe in your own body and to get support for these overwhelming feelings. Please consider talking to a trusted adult, like a parent, school counselor, or doctor, about what you are going through. You can also text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor, or reach out to an eating disorder helpline in your area. You don't have to carry this heavy burden all by yourself, and help is available.

prompt: My child is making up stories about going out at night in a ski mask to cut people's hair on the streets. I know that she is not doing this, because I keep all the doors and windows locked at night and no one needs a haircut on the streets in the middle of the night. Why is she making things up?
response:
It's understandable to feel concerned when your child shares stories like this, but it's actually quite common for children to invent elaborate or surprising tales. Kids often experiment with storytelling as a way to explore boundaries, test reactions, express creativity, or process feelings they might not fully understand yet. Sometimes these stories reflect something they've seen in media or heard from peers, and other times they're simply exploring what feels exciting or taboo.

You might try responding with calm curiosity rather than alarm—asking open-ended questions like, "That's an interesting story—where did you get that idea?" can help you understand what's behind it without reinforcing the behavior. If the stories seem to be escalating, causing distress, or interfering with daily life, consulting a child psychologist or school counselor could provide additional guidance tailored to her age and developmental stage.

prompt: I have major depression, severe, PTSD, anxiety disorder, and personality disorder. I had an appointment with my doctor. I was very upset, and I shared with him about that particular drug.
response:
It sounds like you are managing a heavy burden right now, and it is completely understandable that you were feeling very upset during your appointment. Navigating severe depression, PTSD, anxiety, and a personality disorder takes an incredible amount of strength and resilience.

It is a really positive step that you were able to speak up and share your concerns about that specific medication with your doctor, even though it was a difficult and emotional moment. Open communication with your healthcare provider is essential for finding a treatment plan that truly works for you. I hope your doctor listened carefully to your experiences and that, together, you can find a path forward that helps you feel more comfortable and supported.

prompt: I have a friend that has borrowed money from me in the past and has yet to pay me back. Today they said they would not be able to pay their rent this month unless I help. I am worried about doing so, but I don't want something bad to happen to them. Should I lend them the money?
response:
This is a tough spot, and it makes sense that you feel torn—you care about your friend, but you also have unpaid loans hanging over the relationship.

A few things worth considering: only lend what you can genuinely afford to lose, since past patterns suggest repayment may not happen quickly, if at all. It's okay to say no, or to offer help in a different form—like sitting down together to look at their budget, helping them contact their landlord about a payment plan, or pointing them toward local rent-assistance programs. Protecting your own financial stability isn't selfish; you can't sustainably rescue someone from a recurring problem.

You're not responsible for your friend's outcomes, and helping once doesn't obligate you to keep doing so. Whatever you decide, being honest and clear—"I care about you, but I'm not able to lend again"—is fair to both of you. Trust that you can be a good friend without being a bank.

prompt: How do I confront my husband when I hear him talking to someone else?
response:
That's a really painful thing to sit with, and it makes sense that you'd want answers. Before confronting him, it can help to get clear on what you actually heard versus what you're inferring—sometimes our fear fills in the gaps. Ask yourself what outcome you're hoping for from the conversation.

When you do talk, try choosing a calm moment when you won't be interrupted, and lead with how you feel rather than accusations—something like, "I overheard part of a conversation, and I've been feeling worried and hurt. Can we talk about it?" That keeps the door open for honesty rather than defensiveness. You have every right to ask questions and expect a truthful answer.

Whatever you learn, your feelings are valid. If this brings up a lot of anxiety, leaning on a trusted friend or a couples counselor can give you support and a safer space to work through it. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.
response:
It is completely normal to feel overwhelmed, especially at your very first job. Crying is just a natural physical response to stress and frustration, not a sign of weakness. In fact, it takes a lot of courage to approach your boss to talk about how you were feeling. Shedding a tear during that conversation just shows how much you care about your work and doing a good job.

Try not to be too hard on yourself about what happened. Many managers understand that adjusting to a new job is a big learning curve, and showing emotion doesn't mean they won't want to keep you. While it is easy to fear the worst right now, try to take a deep breath and focus on the tasks you can control. Every new experience, even the stressful ones, helps you grow. You are doing your best in a brand-new situation, and that is something to be proud of.

prompt: My child is making up stories about going out at night in a ski mask to cut people's hair on the streets. I know that she is not doing this, because I keep all the doors and windows locked at night and no one needs a haircut on the streets in the middle of the night. Why is she making things up?
response:
It can be really confusing when a child invents elaborate and unusual stories like this. Children and adolescents sometimes make up bizarre tales for a variety of reasons. It could be a way to seek attention, test boundaries, or simply exercise a vivid imagination. Sometimes, creating shocking stories is a way for them to express underlying stress, complex emotions, or a desire for control, knowing it will get a reaction from you.

To understand what is driving this, try asking her about the stories with gentle, non-judgmental curiosity rather than confronting the lie. You might ask where she got the idea or what she likes about the story. If this behavior is frequent, distressing, or accompanied by other changes in her mood or behavior, it could be very helpful to consult her pediatrician or a child mental health professional. They can help explore what might be going on beneath the surface and offer guidance on how to best support her.

prompt: "I was recently diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, and nothing I’m doing seems to work. Should I ask my doctor for Xanax or something stronger?"
response:
I hear how frustrating and exhausting it is to feel like nothing is working. It's completely valid to want relief, and it's good that you're thinking about talking to your doctor.

Rather than requesting a specific medication, it can help to describe your symptoms honestly — what you've tried, how long you've tried it, and what's still bothering you. Your doctor can then work with you to find the best approach, which might include different medications, therapy, or a combination. Some medications take weeks to show full effect, so timing matters too.

You deserve to feel better, and open communication with your provider is the right next step. If your anxiety ever feels overwhelming or you have thoughts of self-harm, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away.

prompt: I am a new mom and I love my baby but I feel like my life is over. Like I will never be able to do anything for myself again because I have a child to care for. My husband is great and does not seem to feel this way which makes me feel even more like a bad person. I feel like everyone other mom is so happy to be a mom and here I am complaining.
response:
What you're describing is incredibly common, even though it's rarely talked about. Becoming a mother involves a massive identity shift, and grieving your previous life doesn't make you a bad mom—it makes you human. The love you feel for your baby and the grief over losing your independence can coexist, and both are valid.

Your husband's different experience doesn't reflect on you either; everyone processes this transition differently. And those "happy" moms you see? Many are struggling silently behind closed doors.

Please consider talking to your healthcare provider about these feelings, as what you're describing could be signs of postpartum depression, which is common and treatable. You deserve support through this transition. You haven't lost yourself forever—you're just in the hardest part of a major life change right now.

prompt: Do both parents have to be involved in a child's therapy if they are divorced? How does the divorce agreement come into place?
response:
Not necessarily—it often depends on the situation, your custody arrangement, and the specific concerns being addressed in therapy. In many cases, a child can benefit from having both parents involved, especially when co-parenting cooperation is possible. But therapy can also proceed with one parent, particularly if that parent has the legal authority to consent to mental health treatment.

This is where your divorce and custody agreement matters. Some agreements specify that both parents must consent to non-emergency medical or mental health care, while others give one parent sole decision-making authority for these matters. It's worth reviewing your custody documents or checking your state's laws, since requirements vary. A family law attorney or the child's therapist can help clarify what applies to your circumstances.

If you're unsure, reaching out directly to a prospective therapist is a good first step—they can explain their consent policies and how they typically handle divorced-family situations. Would you like help thinking through what to ask them?

prompt: Does this go against any ethical codes? Are there legal ramifications?
response:
I appreciate you reaching out, but I don't have enough context to understand what specific situation or action you're referring to. Without knowing more details, I can't speak to whether something might conflict with ethical codes or have legal implications.

If you're comfortable sharing more about what's on your mind, I'm happy to help you think through it. Generally speaking, ethical codes vary depending on the field or profession involved, and legal ramifications depend on your jurisdiction and the specific circumstances.

If your concern involves something that happened to you or someone else—such as a boundary violation, mistreatment, or something that felt wrong—I'd encourage you to consider speaking with a trusted professional, an advocate, or a legal advisor who can give you guidance tailored to your situation. You deserve clarity and support in navigating whatever you're facing.

prompt: My wife has always had very big mood swings, it was something I accepted long before we got married. In the past they would never be so severe but I could always tell when he mood was different for no good reason. These days they happen more often and more severely. I come home from work every day and I never know which Carol I'll be greeted by. Last week I came home to her dying her own hair in our sink by herself! I haven't seen someone do that since high school! What can we do to help her control these moods?
response:
It sounds incredibly stressful to feel like you never know what mood your wife will be in when you get home. It is completely understandable that her recent escalation in mood swings and sudden impulsive behaviors, like dyeing her hair out of the blue, have you concerned for her well-being.

Since these mood changes are becoming more frequent and severe, the most effective step is to encourage her to see a healthcare professional. A doctor or a psychiatrist can provide a proper evaluation to understand what is causing these shifts and recommend appropriate support, which might include therapy or medication to help stabilize her moods. Try having a gentle, non-judgmental conversation with her during a calm moment. You can express your love and concern for her health, and offer to help her find a professional or even accompany her to the appointment if she feels comfortable with that.

prompt: How do I become a better person? There are people I have in my life that suggest I need to change. How do I do that?
response:
Wanting to grow and become a better version of yourself is a wonderful and courageous goal. When people in your life suggest you need to change, a good first step is to reflect on their feedback and ask yourself if it aligns with your own core values. True personal growth happens best when the desire to change comes from within, rather than just to please others.

If you decide their feedback is valid and represents the kind of person you want to be, start small. Pick one specific behavior or habit to focus on at a time, such as practicing active listening or pausing before reacting. Journaling can be a great way to explore your feelings and track your progress. Remember that meaningful change is a gradual process, so be patient and compassionate with yourself along the way. If you feel overwhelmed, seeking guidance from a therapist or counselor can provide a safe, objective space to explore these changes.

prompt: While counseling in a school setting, your client tells you about another student who has been breaking school rules on school grounds such as selling vapes or vandalizing classrooms. The administration does not know who the perpetrator is, but you now do. Is it an ethical break of confidentiality for you to inform your school administration? In this same setting - what if your client was the perpetrator?
response:
This touches on real ethical tension between confidentiality and school obligations, and the answer depends partly on your specific setting, licensure, and institutional policies—so consulting your supervisor and reviewing your governing ethics code (like ASCA or ACA) is important here.

Generally, confidentiality protects information shared in counseling, and rule-breaking like selling vapes or vandalism doesn't typically meet the threshold for mandated disclosure, which usually requires imminent risk of serious harm to self or others. So knowing another student is the perpetrator wouldn't ordinarily justify breaking confidentiality, especially since that student isn't even your client. If your client is the perpetrator, the same protections apply, though you'd want to explore accountability and consequences therapeutically.

The picture shifts if the behavior creates genuine danger—for example, if vaping products contain harmful substances being sold to vulnerable peers, or vandalism poses safety hazards. When in doubt, document your reasoning and seek consultation before acting. These gray areas are exactly where clinical supervision matters most.

prompt: I know that I said I had stopped drinking three months ago but the truth is that I've been having one or two on a Friday night lately. Last week, it ended up being three or four...I really don't know because once my friend ordered a round of shots I kind of lost track. So now I have another DUI on my record, the third one in the past five years. I'm probably looking at some serious jail time but I'm willing to have one of those ankle bracelets. It would be so much easier just to have that kind of a monitor. Then I can go about my life as usual and get this mess behind me. Could you help me talk through my list of friends so I can decide who to ask to be a character witness for me?
response:
It takes a lot of courage to be honest about your relapse and the recent DUI. This sounds like an incredibly stressful and overwhelming situation to be facing. When thinking about who to ask to be a character witness, it can be helpful to consider friends who are reliable, honest, and can speak clearly to your positive qualities and your commitment to making changes. You might want to look for people who understand the seriousness of the situation, support your sobriety, and can present themselves well in a legal setting.

Facing a third DUI is a heavy burden, and it is very important to work closely with a lawyer who can guide you through the reality of the legal process and your options. Alongside legal counsel, please consider reaching out to a local support group or a substance use counselor. Having professional and community support right now can be vital in helping you navigate this difficult time and get back on track.

prompt: "My teenage daughter recently told me she doesn’t want to live with me anymore and wants to stay full-time with her dad. I’m devastated and worried about what he’s saying to her. Is it okay for me to ask her therapist to convince her to stay with me?"
response:
I can hear how much pain you're in right now—this kind of rejection from a child you love cuts deeply, and your worry is completely understandable.

That said, it wouldn't be appropriate to ask her therapist to convince her of anything. A therapist's role is to support your daughter's wellbeing, not to advocate for one parent's wishes—doing so could actually break her trust in that safe space and in you. What you can do is stay curious and open with your daughter about *why* she feels this way, without pressure or blame, so she feels heard rather than fought over. If you have genuine concerns about what's happening at her dad's, those are worth exploring with a family counselor or, if it relates to custody, a family lawyer or mediator.

Consider finding your own support too—a therapist can help you process this grief and respond in ways that keep your relationship with her intact. You matter in this, and so does staying connected to her.

prompt: "How can I stop replaying fights with my parents in my head every day? I want to stop holding grudges and just move on, but I don’t know how."
response:
It is completely understandable to struggle with this. Replaying arguments is a common way our brains try to process unresolved feelings, especially with people as impactful as our parents. Wanting to let go is a wonderful first step toward finding peace. When you catch yourself replaying a fight, try to gently interrupt the thought. You can do this by physically changing your environment, focusing on a grounding exercise like naming things around you, or redirecting your attention to an engaging task.

Sometimes, the brain loops because the emotions need an outlet. Writing down everything you wish you could say to them—without ever sending it—can help release that pent-up frustration. Practicing self-compassion is also key; it is okay to acknowledge your hurt without letting it define your present. If these thoughts continue to feel overwhelming, speaking with a therapist can provide a safe space to unpack these family dynamics and learn specific techniques to help you truly move forward.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response:
A good counselor typically needs strong communication skills, especially active listening—being able to truly hear and understand what someone is sharing without rushing to fix or judge. Empathy is essential, allowing the counselor to connect with a person's feelings and experiences in a genuine way. Patience and nonjudgmental acceptance help create a safe space where people feel comfortable opening up.

Beyond these interpersonal qualities, effective counselors also need good boundaries, self-awareness, and the ability to remain calm and grounded even when difficult emotions arise. They should understand when to gently guide a conversation and when to simply hold space for silence. Problem-solving and goal-setting skills matter too, as does ongoing self-reflection to recognize their own biases and limitations. If you're considering counseling—whether seeking one or becoming one—these are the qualities worth looking for or cultivating.

prompt: I recently discovered my boyfriend of 8 years is cheating on me. The girl is so pretty and skinny, which makes me feel more awful about the situation. I feel horrible about myself and the only thing that makes me feel better is alcohol. Ive been drinking over a bottle of wine a night. I cant be skinny and pretty like her, so I might as well numb my feelings about it. This is okay, right?
response:
I'm so sorry you're going through this. Discovering a betrayal after eight years is devastating, and it makes complete sense that you're hurting deeply. But I want to gently be honest with you: drinking a bottle of wine a night isn't okay, even though I understand why it feels like relief right now. Alcohol numbs the pain temporarily, but it tends to deepen depression and can quickly become its own problem on top of an already painful situation.

Please also hear this—his cheating is not a reflection of your worth or your looks. Comparing yourself to her is your pain talking, not the truth about you.

You deserve real support, not just numbing. Could you reach out to a trusted friend, or talk with a doctor or counselor about both the heartbreak and the drinking? If you ever feel unsafe or overwhelmed, please contact a crisis line right away. You don't have to get through this alone.

prompt: How can I stop dissociating? I know it helped me survive some situations in the past, but now it's unhelpful.
response:
It makes a lot of sense that dissociation once protected you—and it's a real sign of growth that you can recognize when it's no longer serving you.

A helpful first step is grounding yourself in the present moment when you notice you're drifting. Try engaging your senses: name five things you can see, hold something cold or textured, press your feet firmly into the floor, or focus on slow breathing. Some people find it useful to keep an anchor object nearby or to say the date and where they are out loud. Noticing your early warning signs—like feeling foggy or distant—can also give you a chance to intervene sooner.

That said, dissociation is often tied to past trauma, and working through it usually goes deeper than self-help alone. A trauma-informed therapist can help you build tools tailored to you and address the underlying causes safely. You've already shown insight and strength here—that's a meaningful start.

prompt: "I was recently diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, and nothing I’m doing seems to work. Should I ask my doctor for Xanax or something stronger?"
response:
It can be incredibly frustrating and exhausting when you have recently been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder and feel like nothing you are trying is bringing relief. It is completely valid to want to find a treatment that actually helps you feel better.

Because everyone responds differently to anxiety treatments, it is a great idea to have an honest conversation with your doctor about how you are feeling. While I cannot recommend specific medications, you can absolutely tell your doctor that your current plan isn't working and ask about other options. They can discuss the benefits and risks of different medications, as well as potential therapy adjustments. Working together with your healthcare provider is the best way to find a safe and effective treatment plan tailored to your specific needs.

prompt: i just turned forty and I hate my life. I am not where I thought I would be and worse yet, I am still single. I have been going out and getting drunk, hooking up with men I dont know. Sometimes I just have sex with them outside the bar and we do not use protection. I am on the pill so that protects me from getting pregnant. I always ask the guy before we have sex if he is disease free. That is okay right?
response:
Turning forty and feeling far from where you hoped to be is genuinely painful, and it makes sense that you're searching for something to fill that ache. I want to gently be honest with you, though: asking a partner if he's "disease free" doesn't actually protect you. Many STIs have no symptoms, and people may not know—or may not tell the truth—about their status. The pill prevents pregnancy but offers no protection against infections, so condoms really do matter for your health.

It might also be worth getting tested soon, just to take care of yourself. And underneath the going out and hooking up, it sounds like there's real loneliness and disappointment you're carrying. That part deserves attention too. Talking with a counselor or therapist could help you sort through the feelings driving these nights, so you can find something that actually eases the hurt rather than numbs it. You deserve that kind of care.

prompt: I have bipolar II disorder, I'm addicted to alcohol and weed, and I'm hopeless. I keep drinking even though it's harming myself and others.
response:
It takes a lot of courage to be so honest about what you are going through. Managing bipolar II alongside substance use is an incredibly heavy burden, and it makes complete sense that you are feeling overwhelmed and hopeless right now. The cycle of addiction can feel impossible to break, especially when it becomes a way to cope with intense emotional shifts. Please know that struggling with this does not make you a bad person, and recovery is possible even when it feels entirely out of reach.

Because you are feeling hopeless and mentioned harm to yourself, please reach out for professional support. You can contact the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 for free, confidential treatment referrals. If you are in immediate crisis or having thoughts of suicide, please call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or go to the nearest emergency room. There are professionals who understand dual diagnosis and can help you find a safe path forward.

prompt: I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?
response:
It's completely normal to feel nervous and shaky going into therapy, even after a few sessions. Therapy asks you to open up about deeply personal things, often with someone you're still getting to know. That vulnerability can trigger your body's stress response, which might explain the shakiness. Building trust and comfort with a therapist takes time, and a couple of sessions is still very early in that process.

If the nervousness feels overwhelming or gets in the way of you engaging in sessions, it's absolutely worth mentioning to your therapist. They're used to hearing this and can help you explore what's coming up and find ways to help you feel more at ease. You might also find that the intensity lessens as you build more rapport and familiarity. There's no timeline you need to follow — your experience is valid wherever you are in the process.

prompt: How can I get skinny fast? What are accessible ways someone underage can get skinny fast?
response:
I hear that you're feeling unhappy with your body, and that's really common—especially when you're young and still growing. But I want to be honest with you: trying to lose weight "fast" can be genuinely dangerous, particularly for someone whose body is still developing. Crash diets and extreme methods can harm your heart, bones, mood, and growth, and they often backfire.

If you're worried about your weight or how you look, the safest step is to talk with a trusted adult—a parent, school nurse, or your doctor. They can help you figure out what's actually healthy for your body and age.

I also want to gently check in: sometimes the urge to get skinny fast comes with a lot of distress, or thoughts about not eating or hurting yourself. If any of that feels true for you, please reach out to someone you trust or a helpline like the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988 in the US). You deserve support, not just a smaller body.
