prompt: My child is saying they have a friend named "Bob" who has lived over 100 years and is talking to them on a regular basis. "Bob" does not seem to harm them or scare them, but more annoys them. I'm not sure if this is a ghost, a hallucination, or an imaginary friend. What do I do?
response:
It is completely understandable to feel unsure about how to handle this. Imaginary friends are very common in childhood, and kids often create elaborate backstories for them, like being over 100 years old. It is also not unusual for children to find their imaginary friends annoying at times, as they use these characters to process feelings, practice social interactions, or assert boundaries. Since "Bob" isn't scaring or harming your child, this is likely a normal, creative developmental phase.

The best approach right now is to gently ask your child open-ended questions about Bob out of curiosity, without overly encouraging or dismissing him. Keep an eye on your child's overall mood and daily functioning. If "Bob" becomes distressing, or if your child starts showing other concerning behaviors, it is a good idea to consult your pediatrician or a child psychologist. They can help determine if this is just a vivid imagination or something that needs a little more support.

prompt: I have been with my husband for almost 7 years. We got engaged a little after 5 years of being together. I had always been clear that I wanted to get married and I sadly would drop hints about how i wanted him to propose. When he did propose it was during a random vacation that I had planned. I was happy but I couldn't help feeling disappointed too. I had told him numerous times before that I wanted him to do it in front of my friends and family. I know it sounds dumb to be upset but I couldn't help how I was feeling. We are now married but the wedding and ring were also far from what I wanted and it wasn't due to lack of funds. I know this is all material and the marriage is the most important thing but I cant help but get jealous and envious every time I see someone get a proposal or wedding that I had wanted. I cant help my anger because I know we only get one proposal and one wedding. What I wanted will never happen. I have been working on my feelings for the past year and half to get over it. I try to focus on our marriage but every time I see someone have the best proposals and weddings I get upset. I know it is selfish and I know its petty but I just can't control it. It's ruining our relationship because I constantly think about it. Plus, I get mad at him for small things because I am trying to hide the fact that I am so disappointed. Why can't I move on?
response:
Your feelings aren't petty or selfish—they're real, and you're clearly working hard to make sense of them. What you're describing sounds less like being obsessed with material things and more like grief. You had a meaningful vision of these once-in-a-lifetime moments, and when they didn't happen the way you'd hoped, you lost something you can't get back. That kind of loss deserves acknowledgment, not dismissal.

Part of why it's so hard to move on may be that you're carrying it privately, hiding your disappointment and letting it leak out as anger over small things. That secrecy can keep the wound open. It might help to gently share these feelings with your husband—not as blame, but as honesty about what you're grieving so you're not alone in it.

Talking with a couples or individual therapist could also give you tools to process the disappointment and reconnect. You can honor these feelings and still build a marriage that feels meaningful. Both things can be true.

prompt: My 10-year-old daughter has started staring off into space for long periods and doesn’t respond when I call her name. She was outgoing, but now she’s quiet and doesn’t want to play with friends. What could be going on?
response:
It's understandable to feel worried when your daughter's behavior changes so noticeably. The symptoms you're describing — staring off, not responding, social withdrawal, and a shift from outgoing to quiet — could stem from many possible causes, including anxiety, depression, dissociation, a neurological concern, or a response to stress or something difficult she may be processing. Only a qualified professional can properly assess what's happening.

I'd strongly encourage you to reach out to her pediatrician as a first step. They can help evaluate her and refer you to a child psychologist, psychiatrist, or neurologist if needed. In the meantime, try gently checking in with her in a calm, low-pressure way — "I've noticed you seem quiet lately, and I'm here whenever you want to talk." Avoid pressing her for answers, but let her know she's safe and supported. You're doing the right thing by paying attention and seeking guidance.

prompt: My mother has often struggled with depression, and apparently has ever since I was born. I want to help her, but I'm not sure how I can or what exactly is going on. She doesn't have many friends and is afraid of going outside. What could be going on, and how can I support her?
response:
It is incredibly compassionate of you to want to support your mother. Based on what you've described, she may be dealing with chronic depression alongside severe anxiety or agoraphobia, which can make leaving the house and socializing feel genuinely overwhelming. While you cannot diagnose or cure her, your presence alone is a comfort. You can help by offering a listening ear without judgment and gently encouraging her to speak with a doctor or mental health professional. Offering to help her find a therapist who does telehealth appointments might remove the scary barrier of having to go outside.

You can also support her by spending low-pressure time together at home, like watching a movie or sharing a meal. Please remember that supporting a parent with long-term mental health struggles can be heavy, so it is just as important to set boundaries and seek support for yourself. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: I had a panic attack at a friend's birthday party. Instead of her or anyone trying to help, my friend instead recorded a video and posted it on TikTok and now my panic attack has gone viral. Should I ghost my friend? Should I give her the benefit of the doubt and allow some time for her to apologize and give an explanation?
response:
That sounds like an incredibly painful and violating experience. What your friend did was not okay — recording someone in distress and posting it without consent shows a serious lack of empathy and respect for your privacy. Your anger and hurt are completely valid.

You don't owe her anything right now, including an explanation for why you need space. Whether you choose to ghost or eventually hear her out is entirely your decision — there's no "right" answer. Some people find closure in conversation, while others find peace in walking away. What matters most is protecting your wellbeing. If the video is still up and causing you distress, you can report it to TikTok for violating privacy guidelines. You might also consider reaching out to someone you trust — a counselor, another friend, or a family member — to help you process both the panic attack and this betrayal. Taking time for yourself first, before deciding how to handle the friendship, is a reasonable and healthy choice.

prompt: Nothing I do ever seems to go right. There's always a problem, and I don't have many people I can talk to about it. Sometimes I wonder if things would be better if I wasn't around any longer. What should I do? I feel like other people don't have these same struggles...
response:
It takes real courage to put these feelings into words, and I'm glad you reached out. When you mention wondering if things would be better if you weren't around, that tells me you're carrying a very heavy weight right now. Please know your safety matters. If those thoughts feel strong or you have any urge to act on them, reach out right now to a crisis line—in the US you can call or text 988, and elsewhere emergency services can connect you to help. You don't have to hold this alone.

What you're feeling—like everyone else has it easier—is a common part of struggling, but it doesn't reflect the truth of your worth or your situation. Many people quietly face pain they don't show. Could you reach out to even one person you trust, or a doctor, to start talking about what's been happening? You deserve support, and things can shift even when they feel stuck right now.

prompt: Sometimes I feel like I shouldn’t be this upset because other people have gone through worse. I can’t stop having flashbacks, and I think about the past constantly. I don’t know why I’m still stuck in it. I haven’t been through anything that bad. Am I being dramatic?
response:
You're not being dramatic. Pain isn't a competition, and the fact that others have gone through difficult things doesn't erase or diminish what you experienced. Your mind and body are reacting to something that genuinely affected you—flashbacks and being unable to stop thinking about the past are real, valid responses, not signs of weakness or overreaction.

What you're describing—flashbacks, feeling stuck in the past—can be how trauma shows up, and it's worth taking seriously regardless of how "bad" you judge the event to be. You don't have to have earned your struggle by meeting some threshold of suffering. If these experiences are weighing on you, talking with a therapist, especially one who works with trauma, could really help you understand and work through them. You deserve support just as you are.

prompt: If a couple is seeking couple's therapy, is it ever appropriate for the therapist to meet individually with one member of the couple individually, without the consent of the other participating adult in the couple?
response:
In couples therapy, the relationship itself is considered the primary client. While it is very common for therapists to hold individual sessions with each partner to gather background information or explore specific issues, this should always happen with the knowledge and prior consent of both partners. The guidelines for these individual meetings—including how confidentiality will be handled between partners—are typically established together during the initial informed consent process so everyone understands the boundaries.

Meeting with one partner secretly, without the other partner's consent or knowledge, generally goes against standard ethical practices in couples counseling. Doing so can create a conflict of interest, build unhealthy alliances, and damage the trust necessary for therapy to be effective. If you have concerns about how your therapy is being handled or feel that boundaries are being crossed, it is completely valid to bring this up directly with the therapist to clarify their policies and ensure you feel safe and respected in the process.

prompt: That phrase makes me crazy. It happens anytime I point out something to my husband that he needs to change, such as looking up from his iPad long enough for me to tell him the grandbaby almost pulled the shelf unit over or explaining to him that I got all the things he needs to bake a pie. Another example is when he opens the front door, the dog runs out if he doesn't pick him up. Over and over again, he lets the dog run out, and I am afraid he will get hit by a car.
response:
It sounds incredibly frustrating to feel like your concerns—some of them genuinely about safety, like the shelf or the dog getting hit—aren't being heard or taken seriously. That kind of repeated disconnect can leave you feeling dismissed and alone, even in your own home.

One thing that sometimes helps is naming the specific pattern rather than the individual moments: "When I share something important and get a phrase like that, I feel unheard, and it worries me because some of these are real safety issues." It can also help to pick one or two things that matter most and focus there, rather than everything at once. If these conversations keep going nowhere, a counselor—individually or as a couple—can offer tools for communicating so you both feel respected. You deserve to feel like your voice matters.

prompt: I'm a teenager, and I just got my first job. I am a month and a half in. Yesterday, my boss pushed me to the point where I had to go to the restroom and cry. She didn't see me, and I'm glad, but when I went to talk to her about it today, I let a tear or two come out. I hate it. I feel like they're not going to keep me anymore.
response:
First, congratulations on landing your first job—that's a real accomplishment, and the fact that you're a month and a half in shows you're capable and committed. What you're feeling is completely understandable. Early jobs come with steep learning curves, and it's normal for emotions to run high, especially when you're being pushed hard. Crying doesn't mean you're weak or bad at your job; it means you care.

Showing a tear or two when talking to your boss doesn't automatically mean they'll let you go. Many managers actually respect employees who show up and try to address problems directly, like you did. If you can, focus on what you're learning and how you're improving. It might also help to think through what specifically felt overwhelming, so you can ask for clearer guidance or feedback.

Be kind to yourself—you're growing into this. If the stress starts feeling constant or too heavy, talking to a trusted adult or counselor can really help.

prompt: My therapist is gay so there are no sexual issues here. However, my therapist for six years has made me believe that he cares about me and that we are friends. I have loaned money to him many times, and he always paid me back. I had a medical emergency last weekend and I was heavily medicated. I knew that this therapist came into my home and wrote down my credit card information so he could pay back what he owed me, but this therapist dropped me off and never came again. I don't know what to do.
response:
What you're describing sounds very distressing, and your confusion is completely understandable. A therapist entering your home while you're medicated and writing down your credit card information is a serious boundary violation and may be illegal, regardless of his intent to repay a loan. The professional therapeutic relationship has clear ethical boundaries, and what you've described crosses them significantly.

I'd encourage you to take some protective steps. Consider contacting your credit card company to flag or monitor your account for unauthorized charges. You can also file a complaint with your state or provincial licensing board that oversees therapists, as they investigate ethical violations. If you believe a crime may have occurred, you can contact local police. It may also help to reach out to a trusted friend or family member who can support you right now as you sort through what happened. Please take care of yourself and prioritize your safety and financial security.

prompt: My wife is always accusing me of cheating and telling me that I'm doing things she finds disrespectful even when I don't mean it like that. For example, she gets offended when I call someone at work "sweetheart." I wish I had a penny for every time she accused me of cheating on her. She doesn't, and never will say she was wrong. How do I get her to understand?
response:
That sounds exhausting and painful to navigate. It's hard to feel constantly under suspicion, especially when you don't intend harm.

One approach is to shift the conversation from defending yourself to understanding her feelings. Try saying something like, "I can see this really hurts you, and I want to understand what's behind it." This doesn't mean accepting false accusations, but it may open a more productive dialogue. Her reactions may stem from insecurity, past experiences, or anxiety rather than anything you're actually doing.

That said, you can't force her to see your perspective if she's not ready. Couples counseling could provide a neutral space where both of you feel heard and where patterns like this can be explored safely. A therapist can help facilitate conversations that feel impossible to have on your own.

In the meantime, it's also fair to set gentle boundaries, like expressing that constant accusations are affecting your wellbeing and the relationship. You deserve to feel trusted and respected too.

prompt: My friends makes plans and always cancel. Yet, last week i saw they posted a picture of them out to dinner, but I wasn't invited. I cant believe they would be that rude and immature to plan things behind my back. I am going to send a group text and let them know how immature they are acting
response:
That sounds really hurtful—being repeatedly canceled on and then seeing you were left out would sting anyone. Your feelings are completely valid.

Before you send that group text, it might help to pause. Right now the message would come from anger, and calling them immature could push them further away or turn into a bigger conflict. If you value these friendships, consider reaching out to one person you trust and saying honestly how you felt: "I saw the dinner photo and felt really left out—it's been bothering me." That opens a real conversation instead of a defensive one. And if their pattern of canceling and excluding continues, it's okay to reflect on whether this friendship is giving you what you deserve. Either way, your hurt makes sense, and you're allowed to want to be treated with care.

prompt: How do I ever trust another woman? I have found myself constantly reading between the lines with every other woman that I meet. I am having a difficult time making any sort of connection to anyone because of her deception and willingness to say and do literally anything in order to control my emotions. Once the "relationship" was over, she became extremely abusive and has attempted to intimidate me into silence regarding the many false claims made on her immigration application.
response:
It makes complete sense that you're guarded right now. When someone has deceived and manipulated you the way you describe, your mind learns to scan for danger everywhere—that hypervigilance is your brain trying to protect you from being hurt again. It's not a flaw in you; it's a normal response to a genuinely harmful experience.

Rebuilding trust usually happens slowly, not by forcing yourself to trust everyone, but by letting new people earn it gradually through consistent actions over time. You don't have to open up fully to connect—small, low-stakes interactions can help you relearn that not everyone operates the way she did. Given the abuse and intimidation you mentioned, talking with a therapist who understands manipulative or coercive relationships could really help you process this and protect yourself.

If she's making threats to silence you, keep documentation and consider legal advice about your options. And if you ever feel unsafe, please reach out to local emergency services or a support line. You deserve to feel secure again.

prompt: I have been with my boyfriend for more than a year. He recently got a new job and travels a lot. I’m not used to him being gone all the time. I feel as though he has forgotten about me because he does not talk with me as much and doesn’t keep me up to date on everything that he does throughout the day, which he used to. I feel lost, sad and unwanted. This is really a tough new challenge. I just want to break up with him, but I love him so much. I don’t know why he is acting this way lately. I believe I have separation anxiety. Is there anything that I can do to help me cope with this while he is out of town?
response:
This is a really tough adjustment, and the sadness and loneliness you're feeling make complete sense. When someone's routine changes suddenly, it can feel like the connection itself is fading, even when love is still there. It's worth remembering that his reduced communication may have more to do with a demanding new schedule than his feelings for you.

A helpful first step might be an honest, gentle conversation—not to blame him, but to share how you feel and figure out a check-in rhythm that works for both of you, like a set call each evening. In the meantime, try leaning into things that ground you: friends, hobbies, movement, or anything that fills your days with meaning beyond the relationship. That can ease some of the anxious waiting.

Before deciding on a breakup while you're hurting, give yourself time to see how things settle. If these feelings become overwhelming, talking with a counselor could offer real support. You deserve reassurance and connection—it's okay to ask for it.

prompt: I'm really worried about my mother. She's always been a little disorganized and forgetful but now she's missing doctor's appointments and even locked herself out of the house last week. Dementia runs on her father's side of the family. What other symptoms should I be on the look out for and how do I talk to Mom about going in for a screening when she thinks that she's just having a senior moment now and then?
response:
It's understandable to feel worried, especially with your family history. Beyond forgetfulness, watch for signs like repeating questions or stories, trouble with familiar tasks (managing finances, cooking, following recipes), getting confused about time or place, misplacing items in odd spots, word-finding difficulties, changes in mood or personality, and withdrawing from activities she used to enjoy. Any one of these can have many causes, but a pattern worth noting.

When you talk to her, lead with love rather than diagnosis. Instead of "I think something's wrong," try "I care about you and want us to make sure everything's okay." Framing it as a routine health checkup—like bloodwork or a wellness visit—can feel less threatening. You might offer to go with her, or suggest she raise it with her regular doctor she already trusts. Sometimes hearing it from a physician lands more gently than from an adult child.

If you'd like more guidance, the Alzheimer's Association helpline (1-800-272-3900) offers free, confidential support. Take care of yourself too.

prompt: "My adult daughter told me she needs space from me because she feels I’m too involved in her life. I’ve always been a caring, supportive parent. Is it really fair that she’s pushing me away after everything I’ve done for her? Should I just wait for her to come back around?"
response:
It's clear you love your daughter deeply, and hearing this from her must feel painful and confusing—especially when your involvement came from genuine care. That hurt is completely understandable.

It might help to consider that her needing space isn't a rejection of your love or a denial of everything you've given her. Adult children sometimes need room to build their own independence, and that need can coexist with loving and appreciating you. Rather than only waiting, you could reach out once to let her know you hear her, you respect her request, and you'll be there when she's ready—then genuinely give her that space. Honoring her boundary is often what makes the door open again.

Try to shift the focus from "fairness" toward connection: what does she need to feel respected as an adult? If you can, a calm conversation on her terms may help you both. You're clearly a caring parent, and that care can grow to include trusting her space too.

prompt: I start to think of an issue that doesn't even matter or something bad that happened years ago. Then, I cry, pull at my hair, plug my ears, hit myself, and throw things. In loud public places, I get on edge and start being sarcastic and moody. I have an awful fear of people leaving me (which normally ends up happening) and I feel like I'm too clingy.
response:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of intense emotions, and the way they surface—through hurting yourself, throwing things, and that deep fear of being left—must feel overwhelming and exhausting. What you're describing takes real courage to name, and I want you to know these reactions don't make you broken or "too much." They're signals that something inside you is hurting and looking for relief.

Because you mentioned hitting yourself and pulling your hair, I'd gently encourage you to reach out to a mental health professional who can help you understand what's driving these responses and build safer ways to cope. If the urge to hurt yourself ever feels hard to control, please contact a crisis line—in the US you can call or text 988 anytime.

You deserve support that doesn't leave. Talking to a counselor could be a steady starting point. Would it help to think through how to take that first step?

prompt: I feel so stupid for having been broken up with after only a few weeks. I must have really been a bad girlfriend. I feel like a failure and like something is wrong with me. I hit myself sometimes because I deserve it. How could I have not kept a boyfriend for even a month?
response:
I'm really concerned that you're hitting yourself, and I want you to know that you don't deserve to be hurt by anyone, including yourself. The length of a relationship doesn't measure your worth or whether you were "good enough"—sometimes things just don't work out, and that's not a reflection of you being broken or bad. Please reach out to someone right now, like the Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741) or the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, so you can talk through what you're feeling with someone who can support you.

Your feelings of sadness and frustration make sense, but punishing yourself isn't the answer. You deserve care and compassion, especially from yourself. Please consider reaching out to a trusted friend, family member, or counselor who can be with you right now. You matter, and this painful moment doesn't define you.

prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response:
It is completely understandable that you feel scared right now. Witnessing someone you care about harm themselves during an argument is deeply distressing, and locking yourself in the room was a very smart and safe thing to do. Your physical and emotional safety must always come first.

If you feel that you are in immediate danger or if the situation escalates, please do not hesitate to call emergency services right away. Even if he is only hurting himself, this kind of behavior can be unpredictable. You can also reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) or text "START" to 88788 for confidential support and guidance on how to navigate this safely. Please trust your instincts, stay in a secure space, and consider reaching out to a trusted friend or family member so someone else knows what is happening.

prompt: My new daughter-in-law just informed me that she is smoking marijuana while pregnant because of her morning sickness. I’m in shock and I don’t know how to respond. I just lost my mom, and she was good with advice.
response:
I'm so sorry about the loss of your mom — it's completely understandable that you're missing her guidance right now, especially during such a stressful moment.

Your concern for your daughter-in-law and future grandchild comes from a place of love. Marijuana use during pregnancy can carry potential risks to the baby's development, and most healthcare providers advise against it. The best thing you can do is encourage her to speak openly with her doctor or midwife about her morning sickness. There are safe, medically approved treatments for nausea during pregnancy that her care team can recommend. Approach the conversation gently — she may be struggling more than she's letting on, and morning sickness can be genuinely miserable. You might say something like, "I care about you and the baby so much. Have you talked to your doctor about other options for the nausea?" This keeps the door open without sounding judgmental. You're in a hard spot, and reaching out for guidance — even here — shows how much you care.

prompt: Is it okay for a therapist to abruptly terminate treatment due to extreme countertransference and an unrepairable rupture with the client's legal guardians, even if referrals were provided? Are therapists allowed to terminate treatment for any reason without explanation?
response:
It is completely understandable to feel hurt and confused by an abrupt end to therapy. Ethically, therapists are required to avoid client abandonment, which is why providing referrals is a necessary step when ending treatment. A therapist might need to terminate if they experience severe countertransference or an unmanageable rupture with legal guardians, as these issues can prevent them from providing effective care. In such cases, stepping down is often considered the ethical choice to protect the client.

However, abruptly terminating without any explanation is generally discouraged by professional guidelines. While therapists have the right to end treatment if they cannot provide adequate care, best practices dictate that they should communicate the reasons clearly and offer a proper termination process to minimize harm. If you are feeling left in the dark, it may be helpful to discuss this experience with a new therapist who can help you process this difficult transition and provide the stable support you deserve.

prompt: Or how to send him somewhere that can help him, something like The Baker Act.
response:
It sounds like you're worried about someone and trying to get him help—that shows real care, even when it's hard.

The Baker Act (in Florida) allows for a temporary involuntary evaluation when someone is a danger to themselves or others, or is severely unable to care for themselves due to mental illness. You generally can't file it yourself, but you can help set it in motion. If there's an immediate emergency or he's in danger, call 911 and tell them your concerns—law enforcement can initiate an evaluation. You can also contact a physician, mental health professional, or a mobile crisis team in your area. Calling or texting 988 (the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) can connect you with people who can guide you through the right steps for your situation.

If you can share what state you're in, the process may differ, so local crisis resources are your best bet. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: I can't seem to keep friends in my life, and I've been called narcissistic. I don't think I'm a narcissist. How do I convince people I'm not?
response:
It's painful to feel misunderstood, and to watch friendships slip away without knowing why. That frustration is real, and wanting to be seen accurately makes sense.

Here's a gentle reframe though: focusing on convincing people you're *not* something can be exhausting and often backfires. What tends to help more is getting curious about the pattern itself. When friendships end, is there anything that repeats—feeling unheard, conflicts over needs, difficulty with give-and-take? You don't have to accept a label like "narcissistic," but the fact that it's come up might be worth exploring honestly rather than defending against.

Sometimes an outside perspective helps here. A therapist can offer a nonjudgmental space to look at your relationships and understand what's happening, without the sting of a friend's accusation. That's not about proving anything—it's about building the kind of connections you actually want. You clearly care about people staying in your life, and that caring is a good place to start.

prompt: I get so anxious sometimes I pull my hair out. I almost don't have anymore eyelashes or brows. I feel like a loser for not being able to control this, but I just can't stop. And then I feel even more anxious and bad about myself.
response:
Thank you for sharing something so personal and painful. What you're describing sounds like it could be trichotillomania, a recognized condition where hair pulling becomes a way of coping with anxiety or tension. It's not a weakness or a character flaw—it's a real struggle that many people face, and feeling ashamed about it only adds to the cycle you're describing.

You're caught in a loop: anxiety leads to pulling, pulling leads to shame, and shame fuels more anxiety. That doesn't make you a loser; it makes you human and stuck in something that's genuinely hard to manage alone.

A therapist, particularly one who works with body-focused repetitive behaviors or uses approaches like CBT or habit reversal training, could help you develop tools to interrupt this cycle with compassion rather than punishment. You deserve support that addresses both the pulling and the anxiety underneath it. Please consider reaching out to a mental health professional when you're ready.

prompt: A woman with a history of substance use that includes several treatment programs and relapses discloses to her counselor that the man she has been living with has recently relapsed. She stated that she remains clean but that her partner keeps leaving his drugs out in the open, which has begun to trigger some old cravings. Last night, she said, when she gently challenged him about his relapse and whether he would consider entering treatment, the discussion quickly escalated to the point that he raised his open hand as if he were going to slap her. In today's counseling session, she asks if she could bring him to her next session so that he could hear from a neutral party how his behavior is affecting her own recovery. What would be the most appropriate response from the counselor?
response:
This sounds like a very difficult and potentially unsafe situation, and your safety needs to come first. Given that your partner raised his hand to you, bringing him into your counseling session could put you at risk and isn't something I'd recommend right now. A therapy space should remain a safe, confidential environment for you.

What I'd encourage instead is focusing on your safety and recovery. Let's talk about whether you have a safe place to stay, whether you're comfortable with a safety plan, and what support options are available to you. If you ever feel in immediate danger, please contact emergency services or a crisis line right away. Your recovery and your physical safety are both priorities, and you deserve support that centers on your well-being.

prompt: I have been with my husband for almost 7 years. We got engaged a little after 5 years of being together. I had always been clear that I wanted to get married and I sadly would drop hints about how i wanted him to propose. When he did propose it was during a random vacation that I had planned. I was happy but I couldn't help feeling disappointed too. I had told him numerous times before that I wanted him to do it in front of my friends and family. I know it sounds dumb to be upset but I couldn't help how I was feeling. We are now married but the wedding and ring were also far from what I wanted and it wasn't due to lack of funds. I know this is all material and the marriage is the most important thing but I cant help but get jealous and envious every time I see someone get a proposal or wedding that I had wanted. I cant help my anger because I know we only get one proposal and one wedding. What I wanted will never happen. I have been working on my feelings for the past year and half to get over it. I try to focus on our marriage but every time I see someone have the best proposals and weddings I get upset. I know it is selfish and I know its petty but I just can't control it. It's ruining our relationship because I constantly think about it. Plus, I get mad at him for small things because I am trying to hide the fact that I am so disappointed. Why can't I move on?
response:
It is completely understandable that you are struggling to move on. While you might feel like your disappointment is just about the material aspects of the proposal and wedding, it sounds like the hurt runs much deeper. When you clearly communicate your desires and they are overlooked, it can make you feel unheard and undervalued by your partner. Your lingering anger and jealousy aren't just about a ring or a party; they are likely a natural response to feeling like your husband didn't prioritize what was deeply important to you.

Hiding your disappointment and letting it spill over into small arguments is taking a heavy toll on your marriage. To truly move forward, it might help to have an honest, vulnerable conversation with your husband about why this hurt you so much—focusing on the feeling of not being heard rather than the events themselves. Exploring these feelings with a couples counselor could also provide a safe space to process this resentment and rebuild your connection.

prompt: I've been bulimic for about 6 years now. I'm in my early 20s. I am about to start back to school to become an RN, and I really need to get better once and for all. I lose control of myself and become angry and anxious and just eat and purge. Over and over. Can someone please point me in the right direction for help?
response:
It takes a lot of courage to reach out, and wanting to heal before starting nursing school is a wonderful, positive goal. Dealing with bulimia, anxiety, and anger for six years is incredibly exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you want to break this cycle once and for all. Please know that recovery is absolutely possible, and you deserve to feel at peace with yourself.

To get started, reaching out to a therapist or medical professional who specializes in eating disorders is a crucial step. You can contact the National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline at 866-662-1235 to find treatment options, specialists, and support groups in your area. Additionally, if you ever feel overwhelmed by anxiety or the urge to purge and need immediate support, you can text HOME to 741741 to connect with the Crisis Text Line. You are taking a brave first step toward a healthier future, and there is professional support available to help you get there.

prompt: My four year old daughter has been struggling with her milestones for as long as I can remember. Potty training has been an absolute nightmare, she refuses to go and will even sit on the toilet crying for half an hour while refusing to "go" at all. In fact she's never once used the toilet correctly. She gestures at herself in the mirror, looking at herself is one of her favorite hobbies, but anytime one of us is looking at her it feels like she's looking through us instead of at us. We were hoping that a half day at preschool would be helpful for her to develop out of these issues but they seem to persist. What can we try next?
response:
It sounds incredibly stressful to navigate these challenges, and it is completely understandable that you are looking for the best way to support your daughter. The behaviors you mentioned—such as the intense struggles with potty training, her fascination with the mirror, and the feeling that she is looking through you rather than making eye contact—are very important observations. Since preschool hasn't eased these concerns, the most helpful next step is to share these specific details with her pediatrician.

A pediatrician can offer a developmental screening and may refer you to a pediatric occupational therapist or a developmental specialist. These professionals can help determine if there are underlying sensory processing differences or developmental delays contributing to her struggles. They can also provide you with tailored, gentle strategies to make milestones like potty training less distressing for both of you. You are doing a wonderful job advocating for her by paying such close attention to her unique needs.

prompt: I feel like this counseling has helped with my self-esteem and not blaming myself so much for all of my problems but I still go on a drinking binge at least once a month. What are the quickest ways for me to cut down on alcohol, maybe even get sober once and for all?
response:
It's great that counseling has helped with your self-esteem and self-blame—that's real progress worth acknowledging. For cutting down on alcohol, some approaches that can help include identifying your triggers and planning ahead for high-risk situations, setting clear limits before you drink, removing alcohol from your home, and finding alternative activities or coping strategies for stress. Connecting with support groups like SMART Recovery or AA can also provide structure and community.

That said, since you're looking to make significant changes to your drinking patterns, it's worth discussing this with a healthcare provider or your current counselor. They can help you explore whether medical support might be appropriate, especially since reducing alcohol use can sometimes involve withdrawal risks depending on your patterns. They can also help you build a personalized plan that fits your life. You don't have to figure this out alone, and reaching out for that kind of support is a strength, not a weakness.

prompt: If you have a client who works at a factory with large machinery and he discloses he is alcoholic and drinks before every shift would it be acceptable for the counselor to report him to his job due to this dangerous behavior?
response:
This is a genuinely difficult ethical situation, and the answer depends on your jurisdiction, licensing board rules, and specific confidentiality laws.

Generally, counselor confidentiality is strong, but most ethical codes and laws include exceptions for imminent, serious danger to the client or others. Operating heavy machinery while intoxicated can create a foreseeable risk of serious harm—not only to him but to coworkers. Whether that rises to a legally reportable "duty to warn/protect" threshold varies, and reporting to an employer is different from warning an identifiable third party at risk.

Before acting, I'd strongly encourage you to consult your specific code of ethics (ACA, NASW, APA, etc.), your state or country's confidentiality and duty-to-protect statutes, and ideally a supervisor, attorney, or your licensing board. Clinically, you'd typically first address it directly with the client, assess risk, discuss safety and treatment options, and document thoroughly. If you're facing this right now with immediate danger present, err toward preventing imminent harm and get supervisory/legal guidance quickly.

prompt: My 10-year-old daughter has started staring off into space for long periods and doesn’t respond when I call her name. She was outgoing, but now she’s quiet and doesn’t want to play with friends. What could be going on?
response:
It is completely understandable to be worried about these sudden changes in your daughter. Her symptoms could point to a few different things. Staring off into space and being unresponsive to her name can sometimes be a medical issue, such as absence seizures, which are brief periods of lost awareness. At the same time, her shift from being outgoing to quiet and withdrawing from friends could indicate an emotional or psychological struggle, such as anxiety, depression, bullying, or a response to a stressful event.

Because these changes are significant and involve both behavioral and potential physical symptoms, it is very important to have her evaluated by a pediatrician as soon as possible. A doctor can help rule out any medical conditions and guide you toward a child psychologist or counselor if the root cause is emotional. In the meantime, continue offering her a gentle, pressure-free environment so she knows you are there to support her whenever she is ready.

prompt: I've been hearing voices telling me to do things I don't want to do. What should I do to make them stop?
response:
Hearing voices that tell you to do things you don't want to do sounds frightening, and I'm glad you're reaching out. Please take this seriously and seek help right away. If you feel like you might act on what the voices are saying or if you're in any danger, please call emergency services (911) or go to your nearest emergency room immediately.

You can also reach out to a crisis line like the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or text HOME to 741741 to connect with someone who can support you right now. Please also contact a healthcare provider or mental health professional as soon as possible — they can help you understand what's happening and find treatment that can help. You don't have to manage this alone, and there are people who want to help you feel safe.

prompt: About 3 years ago or so I was skinny, but I was still ugly. I really do want to change that but I've tried 3 times. Now can I try but don't stop. At school I get bullied about my weight and my ugliness and I have been bullied my whole life that I believe them. How can I stop thinking about them and don't let it get in my head? My parents said I don't weight that much but, they do think I am fat but, they tell me I am not. I told my parents that I need to go to a therapist, but they think I am fine and I think they don't want to deal with it.
response:
I am so sorry you have been dealing with bullying for so long. It is completely understandable that hearing those hurtful things repeatedly has made you start to believe them, but please know that their words do not define your worth. People who bully often do so out of their own insecurities, and their cruelty is a reflection of them, not you. You deserve to feel comfortable and confident in your own skin, and learning to separate your true value from their negativity takes time and support.

It is incredibly frustrating when you ask for help, like seeing a therapist, and your parents don't recognize how much you are struggling. Since your parents are hesitant right now, consider reaching out to a school counselor, a trusted teacher, or a doctor. They can offer you a safe space to talk about these feelings and might even be able to help explain to your parents why professional support is so important for your well-being. Please don't give up on advocating for yourself.

prompt: Stefan, a full-time college student working 30-hours per week, just failed two mid-term exams. Although he needs to keep his job to pay the bills, earning a degree is his top priority. In today's counseling session he disclosed that when he approached his supervisor about reducing his hours until the end of the semester, the supervisor brushed off his request and said that there was no one else who could be relied upon to open up and close the shop right now. Stefan has been working on becoming more assertive and asks his counselor for suggestions on how best to make a case with his supervisor for cutting back to 20 hours a week. What would be the most appropriate response from the counselor?
response:
An appropriate response would first validate Stefan's dedication to his education and his progress in wanting to practice assertiveness. It is completely understandable that he feels overwhelmed balancing a 30-hour work week with his studies, especially after a setback with his exams.

To help him make his case, you might suggest that Stefan schedule a formal, dedicated time to speak with his supervisor, rather than bringing it up in passing. He can practice using clear, firm "I" statements, such as, "I value my job here, but I must reduce my hours to 20 per week to succeed in my classes." To address the supervisor's concern about opening and closing the shop, Stefan could offer a collaborative but firm solution, like helping train another employee for those shifts over the next week. This approach allows him to hold his boundaries and prioritize his degree while still showing professionalism and respect for the business's needs.

prompt: Would it ever be appropriate if a therapist utilized second hand information to confront a client?
response:
That's a thoughtful question, and the answer really depends on context.

Generally, ethical therapists rely on what you share directly and work to build trust rather than "confronting" you with information gathered elsewhere. However, there are situations where outside information might come up appropriately—for example, in family or couples therapy where multiple people are involved, or when a therapist has a genuine safety concern (like risk of harm to you or someone else). Even then, a skilled therapist usually raises it transparently, explaining where the concern comes from and inviting your perspective rather than ambushing you.

If this happened to you and it felt jarring or like a breach of trust, that reaction is worth paying attention to. You have every right to ask your therapist directly: "Where did that come from, and why are you bringing it up?" A good therapist will welcome that conversation. If the answer doesn't sit right with you, it's okay to reconsider the fit.

Is there a specific situation prompting this?

prompt: It's really hard to not have negative feelings about friends who don't put any effort into nourishing our relationship.
response:
It makes complete sense that you'd feel hurt or frustrated when friendship feels one-sided. Wanting effort in return isn't demanding—it's a reasonable hope for connection, and noticing that imbalance shows how much you value closeness.

Sometimes it helps to gently name what you need, either to yourself or directly to a friend, and see how they respond. Their reaction can tell you a lot about where to invest your energy. It's also okay to let some relationships become lighter while giving your attention to people who show up for you. Your negative feelings aren't a flaw; they're information about what matters to you. Be kind to yourself as you figure out what feels right.

prompt: I think I'm annoying and bothersome, but my girlfriend says I'm just fine. I don't think so, I think I'm stressing everyone else out
response:
It sounds really painful to carry that belief about yourself, especially when it conflicts with what someone close to you is saying. Sometimes our inner critic can be much harsher than reality, and it can be hard to accept reassurance even when it's genuine.

Your girlfriend's perspective matters — she knows you and is telling you that you're not a burden. It's okay to not fully believe that right away, but try to stay open to the possibility that she might be seeing something you can't. If these feelings are persistent and affecting your relationships or wellbeing, talking to a mental health professional could help you understand where this self-critical voice comes from and how to quiet it. You deserve to feel okay being yourself.

prompt: I just wanted to get to know one so I can hear about their college experience and the courses they took. I also wanted to know if they enjoy their job and how long they were in school.
response:
It sounds like you are looking to do an informational interview to learn more about a specific career path. As an AI, I don't have personal college experiences, coursework, or a career history to share with you. However, reaching out directly to professionals in the field you are interested in is a fantastic way to learn about their educational journey and day-to-day work life.

You might consider connecting with people through professional networks, reaching out to a local college's career center, or asking teachers or mentors if they know anyone you could speak with. Many professionals are very happy to share their experiences, discuss how long they were in school, and offer guidance to someone who is eager to learn about their field.

prompt: My best friend wants to stop being friends with me and it's making me feel depressed and anxious. She doesn't care how I feel. Sometimes she says she is open to working things out, but most of time she is distant and angry. Do I have to just accept it if she doesn't want to be my friend anymore, even after 20 years?
response:
I'm so sorry you're going through this. Losing a close friend after 20 years is deeply painful, and your feelings of depression and anxiety make complete sense. This is a significant loss.

The mixed signals — sometimes open, often distant — make it harder because you can't find closure. While you can't force someone to stay in a friendship, you *can* advocate for one honest, clear conversation where you ask for a direct answer about where things stand. After that, if she chooses to step away, accepting it — painful as it is — is ultimately about protecting your own wellbeing. You deserve relationships where you feel valued and where your feelings matter.

Please consider talking to a counselor or therapist who can help you process this grief. Losing a long friendship can feel like mourning, and you don't have to carry that weight alone. Be gentle with yourself right now.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this—racing thoughts, poor sleep, and constant anxiety are exhausting, especially when medications haven't been an option for you. That's a lot to carry, and it makes sense you feel like a wreck.

Since medicines have caused hard reactions, it's worth asking your doctor about non-medication approaches, and mentioning your head injury history—sometimes anxiety and sleep issues after a head injury need a specialized evaluation (like a neurologist). In the meantime, some people find slow breathing helpful: breathe in for four counts, hold briefly, then exhale slowly for six. Gentle movement, limiting screens before bed, and grounding techniques (naming things you can see, hear, and touch) can also ease a racing mind.

You don't have to figure this out alone. If your anxiety ever feels unbearable or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line (call or text 988 in the US) right away. You deserve real support and relief.

prompt: Can a therapist have a client admitted to an eating disorder treatment center if the client does not want to go?
response:
In most cases, a therapist cannot force a client into eating disorder treatment without their consent unless the client is in immediate, life-threatening danger. If someone's eating disorder has caused severe medical instability—such as dangerously low weight, electrolyte imbalances, or risk of organ failure—a therapist or medical professional may initiate an emergency hold or hospitalization to protect their life. This process varies depending on local laws and the specific circumstances.

If you're navigating this situation, it's important to know that treatment is generally most effective when someone is willing to participate. If you're concerned about yourself or someone else, reaching out to a healthcare provider, a crisis line, or an eating disorder helpline can help clarify options and provide guidance. You deserve support and care, and there are people who can help you explore what feels right.

prompt: I have been feeling really upset recently about every little thing and worried constantly that something bad is going to happen. My mom is not concerned and won't get me help. Is this normal to struggle with?
response:
It sounds really hard to feel constantly worried and upset, especially when you're not getting the support you need from your mom. What you're describing — persistent worry and feeling overwhelmed by small things — is something many people struggle with, and your feelings are valid. It's not your fault, and you deserve to feel better.

Even if your mom isn't helping right now, there are other options. You can talk to a school counselor, teacher, or another trusted adult who can help you figure out next steps. You can also reach out to a youth helpline or text line (like texting HOME to 741741 in the U.S.) to talk with someone who can listen and help you find resources. If you ever feel like you're in crisis or unsafe, please contact emergency services or a crisis line right away. You don't have to handle this alone.

prompt: I'm really worried about my mother. She's always been a little disorganized and forgetful but now she's missing doctor's appointments and even locked herself out of the house last week. Dementia runs on her father's side of the family. What other symptoms should I be on the look out for and how do I talk to Mom about going in for a screening when she thinks that she's just having a senior moment now and then?
response:
It's understandable to feel worried, and you're right to pay attention to these changes. Beyond memory issues, watch for difficulty with familiar tasks, confusion about time or place, mood or personality changes, trouble finding words, poor judgment, withdrawal from activities, and problems with planning or problem-solving.

When talking with your mom, try framing it around her wellbeing rather than a diagnosis. You might say, "I love you and want to make sure you're healthy. Since you've missed some appointments, let's go together for a check-up." Offering to accompany her can reduce anxiety. Some people respond better to the idea of a "baseline cognitive check" rather than "dementia screening." If she's resistant, a trusted doctor or family friend might help. Early evaluation can rule out reversible causes like medication interactions or vitamin deficiencies, and if it is dementia, early planning makes a real difference.

prompt: My husband took a job out of state for the next year and seems to be a different person. Before, he worked and slept, and on off days, he'd stay home because he didn't want to do anything else. Now he's going out with friends several nights a week while I'm still home working a 50 hours a week job and taking care of two kids by myself. He's suddenly saying he misses me and wants me to be his adored wife, but the whole time, I'm remembering how I've been emotionally starving for the last five years.
response:
That's a painful contradiction to sit with—now that he's suddenly available and affectionate, you're being asked to give warmth you didn't receive when you needed it most. It makes sense that you'd feel resentful, or even numb, rather than instantly ready to reconnect. Five years of emotional starvation doesn't disappear because he's finally noticing you.

Your feelings are valid, and so is your exhaustion. You're carrying a full-time job and two kids alone while he's rediscovering a social life. It's fair to want acknowledgment of that imbalance before you can open up again. You might tell him honestly that you can't just flip a switch, and that you need him to understand the years you spent feeling unseen. If you can, consider couples counseling to help both of you talk through this gap. You deserve a partnership where your needs matter too—not just when it's convenient for him.

prompt: How do I cope with losing my mom?
response:
I am so incredibly sorry for the loss of your mom. Losing a parent is one of the most profound and painful experiences, and it is completely normal to feel overwhelmed, lost, or a mix of many different emotions right now. Please know that there is no "right" timeline or way to grieve. It is a deeply personal journey, and it is okay to just take things one day, or even one hour, at a time.

As you navigate this heavy time, try to be as gentle with yourself as possible. Allow yourself to feel whatever comes up without judgment, and lean on trusted friends or family members who can listen. You might also find comfort in honoring her memory in small ways, like writing her a letter or doing something she loved. If the grief ever feels too heavy to carry alone, reaching out to a grief counselor or a support group can provide a safe, understanding space to process your feelings.

prompt: How do I grow into a new person? What are some ways I can help myself?
response:
Growing into a new person is a beautiful and courageous journey. It often starts with small, intentional steps — reflecting on what matters to you, setting gentle goals, and being patient with yourself as you change. You might try journaling to understand your thoughts, exploring new interests to discover what energizes you, or practicing self-compassion when things feel difficult. Growth rarely happens in a straight line, and that's okay.

Surrounding yourself with supportive people, reading books that inspire you, or speaking with a counselor can also help you gain clarity and tools along the way. Change doesn't require a dramatic overhaul — it's built from consistent, kind choices that align with the person you want to become. Trust that you already have the capacity within you to grow, even if the path forward feels uncertain right now. You deserve to invest in yourself, and every small step counts.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response:
A good counselor relies on a foundation of strong interpersonal skills to create a safe, supportive, and healing environment. The most essential skill is active listening, which means truly hearing and understanding what a person is saying rather than just waiting to respond. Empathy is equally crucial, allowing the counselor to connect with a client's feelings and validate their experiences. Additionally, a good counselor must maintain a non-judgmental attitude, ensuring people feel completely accepted regardless of what they share.

Effective communication and the ability to ask thoughtful, open-ended questions are also important, as they help guide individuals toward their own insights and solutions. Finally, a strong counselor knows how to set healthy boundaries and maintain strict confidentiality, which builds the deep trust necessary for effective therapy.

prompt: "My ex-husband is taking me back to court for custody and I need evidence to show he’s emotionally abusive. Can my child’s therapist testify in court on my behalf and share details of what my child said in therapy?"
response:
Going through a custody battle, especially when emotional abuse is involved, is incredibly stressful. Whether your child's therapist can testify depends on your local laws, the therapist's professional guidelines, and the consent agreements you signed. Many therapists have strict policies against testifying in custody disputes because sharing session details can break the child's trust and damage the safe space they need for healing. Instead of the treating therapist, courts often rely on a specialized custody evaluator or a Guardian ad Litem to assess the situation.

Because I cannot provide legal advice, it is very important to consult with a family law attorney who can guide you on the best way to legally present evidence of emotional abuse in your jurisdiction. You may also want to have an open conversation with the therapist about their boundaries regarding court involvement, so you know exactly what to expect and how best to support your child through this difficult process.

prompt: I self-harm, and I stop for awhile. Then when I see something sad or depressing, I automatically want to self-harm.
response:
Thank you for sharing this with me. It takes courage to talk about self-harm, and I want you to know that your feelings are valid. What you're describing—being triggered by sad or depressing things—is very common. Our brains can create strong associations between emotional pain and self-harm as a coping mechanism, and those patterns can resurface even after we've stopped for a while.

When you notice that urge coming on, try to create a small buffer between the trigger and your response. This could be reaching out to someone you trust, doing something physical like holding ice or snapping a rubber band, or simply removing yourself from the situation. Consider speaking with a mental health professional who can help you develop personalized coping strategies and work through the underlying emotions. You can also reach out to a crisis line like 988 (in the US) anytime you need support. You deserve care and help through this.

prompt: As a child, my parents injured my brother, so they went to prison. I was there when he had gotten hurt, but I can't seem to remember. I also can't remember being with them quite well. It's a blur.
response:
Thank you for sharing something so deeply painful. What you're describing—blurry or missing memories around traumatic events—is actually a very common response to childhood trauma. Our minds can shield us from overwhelming experiences by making those memories difficult to access. This doesn't mean anything is wrong with you; it's a protective response.

That said, carrying the weight of what happened to your brother and the complicated feelings around your parents can be incredibly heavy, especially when the memories feel fragmented or unclear. Working through this with a trauma-informed therapist could help you process what you do remember, understand your reactions, and find ways to cope with the gaps. You deserve support in navigating this, and you don't have to carry it all alone.

prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response:
That sounds really frightening, and it makes complete sense that you were scared. Seeing someone you care about hurt themselves during an argument is upsetting, and locking yourself in a room was a reasonable way to protect yourself and get some space. You did nothing wrong.

Right now, please focus on your own safety. If things feel unsafe or escalate again, don't hesitate to call emergency services or a trusted friend or family member who can be with you. If your boyfriend is having thoughts of harming himself, he can reach a crisis line—in the US, that's 988 (call or text). When things are calm, it may help to talk with someone you trust about what happened, since this kind of moment can be a lot to carry alone. How are you feeling right now, in this moment?

prompt: Recently, my friend has been forgetting things frequently, like what day and year it is, or feeding his pets. He never used to be like this. Is something wrong, or am I just paranoid?
response:
It's caring of you to notice these changes in your friend—you're not being paranoid. Forgetting things like the date, or basic routines like feeding pets, especially when it's a clear shift from how he used to be, is worth paying attention to. Sudden or noticeable memory changes can have many causes, some very treatable, so it's a good idea for him to get checked out by a doctor.

If you can, gently encourage him to see his primary care physician, who can evaluate what's going on. If you're close with his family, you might mention what you've observed so someone can help him follow up. And if he ever seems confused in a way that puts his safety at risk right now—like wandering, forgetting to eat for days, or seeming very disoriented—don't hesitate to reach out to someone who can check on him promptly. Trusting your instincts here is a good thing.

prompt: How can I work to find more meaning in my day-to-day life?
response:
Finding more meaning often starts with small, intentional shifts rather than big life overhauls. Try noticing what activities make you lose track of time or leave you feeling genuinely engaged—those are clues to what matters to you. Connecting with people, contributing to something beyond yourself (even in small ways like helping a neighbor), and aligning your daily choices with your core values can all deepen a sense of purpose.

It can also help to reflect regularly: a few minutes each evening asking "What felt meaningful today, and why?" builds awareness over time. Meaning tends to grow from action and connection, so experiment with new things and pay attention to what resonates. Be patient with yourself—this is an ongoing process, not a destination. If you ever feel persistently empty or low, talking with a counselor can offer helpful support along the way.

prompt: I would like to be able to have more positive relationships in the present.
response:
It's wonderful that you're focusing on building more positive relationships — that desire itself shows real self-awareness and hope. Meaningful connections often start with small steps: being curious about others, practicing active listening, and allowing yourself to be a little vulnerable when it feels safe to do so. Sometimes it also helps to reflect on what qualities you value most in relationships, so you can seek those out intentionally.

It's also okay to go at your own pace. Building trust and connection takes time, and every small interaction — a kind word, a moment of genuine presence — can be a step toward the relationships you want. If you find old patterns or fears getting in the way, consider talking with a counselor or therapist who can help you explore those barriers in a supportive space. You deserve fulfilling connections, and the fact that you're reaching for them matters.

prompt: My daughter Laila just started third grade at a new school and comes home talking about her new friend, Kendra. Kendra sounds like a fun girl, so I suggested that we talk to Kendra's parents about having her come over to our house. When I spoke to the teacher, however, it turns out there is no one named Kendra at school. Laila's never had an imaginary friend before and has had a good grasp of reality versus fantasy for the past couple years. I'm wondering what might be going on for her to be regressing like this.
response:
It is completely understandable to feel concerned about Laila's new imaginary friend, especially since she hasn't had one before. Starting a new school is a major transition, and children often find creative ways to cope with the stress, loneliness, or overwhelming feelings that come with it. Rather than a regression, creating "Kendra" might simply be Laila's way of navigating this big change, self-soothing, and practicing social interactions in a safe, controllable way.

You might try gently asking Laila how she is feeling about her new school and classmates, focusing on her emotions rather than confronting her about Kendra's existence right away. Giving her a safe space to share her feelings can help her process this transition. If you notice other signs of distress, or if she seems disconnected from reality in other areas of her life, it could be very helpful to consult her pediatrician or a child counselor for professional guidance.

prompt: I been having anger problems a lot lately. It only takes one word wrongly said to set me off. I use to not be like this until I got with my soon-to-be husband. I think his mood and rage/anger problems have rubbed off on me a lot. I don't get nearly as bad as he does, but I yell almost constantly and I can't seem to just stop. I have two young babies that have to hear this, and I don't want my girls growing up with a mommy like I have been lately. I just don't know how to get back to my old self.
response:
It takes a lot of courage to recognize this change in yourself and want a healthier environment for your daughters. It is very common to absorb the emotional climate of our surroundings. Living with a partner who struggles with intense rage can put your own nervous system on high alert, making you feel constantly on edge and quick to react. You are not a bad mother for struggling with this; the fact that you want to find your way back to your old self shows how much you care.

Speaking with a mental health professional could be incredibly helpful. A therapist can teach you grounding techniques to manage your anger in the moment and help you navigate the stress of your home environment. Because you mentioned your partner's rage gets very bad, please remember that your well-being is paramount. If you ever feel unsafe or overwhelmed, please reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE or text "START" to 88788. You and your babies deserve a peaceful home.

prompt: "I’m tired of always feeling like I’m not good enough because of how my ex treated me. What steps can I take to rebuild my self-esteem and stop overthinking the past?"
response:
It is completely understandable to feel exhausted from carrying the weight of how your ex treated you. Healing from a relationship that damaged your self-worth takes time, and recognizing that their behavior was a reflection of them—not your true value—is a powerful first step toward healing.

To start rebuilding your self-esteem, try practicing self-compassion by speaking to yourself the way you would support a close friend. When you catch yourself overthinking the past, gently redirect your focus to the present moment through grounding exercises or by engaging in an activity that brings you joy. Reconnecting with your own interests and surrounding yourself with uplifting people can help you rediscover your strengths outside of that relationship. If these thoughts continue to feel overwhelming, speaking with a mental health professional can provide a safe space to process the past and develop personalized strategies for moving forward.

prompt: My husband and I have been together since high school. We have been married going on for nearly ten years, and we have three beautiful children. A few weeks ago, my husband decided he need some time apart and moved over to his dad’s for a while. He comes home to see the kids and acts like there is not too much wrong. Can this marriage be saved or is it too late? He said he would go to counseling, so I don't think he has given up.
response:
It sounds like you are going through a very confusing and painful time, especially after being together for so long and sharing a family. It is completely understandable to feel anxious about the future of your marriage right now.

The fact that your husband is willing to go to counseling is a very positive sign. It shows that he is open to working on the relationship and communicating, which means it is certainly not too late to try and save your marriage. Couples counseling can provide a safe, neutral space for both of you to explore what led to this separation, understand his need for space, and figure out how you might bridge the gap. Taking this step together is a great way to gain clarity. Focusing on that process and taking things one day at a time is a wonderful way to support yourself and your family right now.

prompt: How do I cope with losing my mom?
response:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your mom. Grief is deeply personal, and there's no right or wrong way to move through it. It's okay to feel a wide range of emotions — sadness, anger, confusion, even moments of peace — sometimes all in the same day. Be gentle with yourself and allow yourself to feel whatever comes up without judgment.

Some people find comfort in talking about their loved one, creating rituals or keepsakes, or connecting with others who understand loss. Supporting yourself with basics like rest, nourishment, and movement can also help, even when it feels hard. If you're struggling to cope or feeling overwhelmed, reaching out to a grief counselor or a support group can make a real difference. You don't have to carry this alone. If you ever feel like you're in crisis or having thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or someone you trust right away. Your feelings matter, and support is available.

prompt: I struggle with anxiety all the time -- at school, at home, in social situations. How can I make this better?
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to carry that weight of anxiety with you everywhere you go, whether you are at school, at home, or with friends. Please know that you are not alone in feeling this way, and it is completely okay to seek support to find some relief.

When anxiety feels overwhelming, practicing grounding techniques can sometimes help bring your focus back to the present. Taking slow, deep breaths or focusing on specific things you can see and hear around you can help signal to your body that you are safe. Because this anxiety is affecting so many areas of your life, reaching out to a school counselor, a doctor, or a mental health professional could be a very helpful next step. They can work with you to understand what is driving the anxiety and help you build personalized strategies to feel more at ease.

prompt: I see that you've been glancing down at my arms. Yeah, those are some new scratches on both sides. Sometimes I don't even notice that I'm scratching myself until the skin breaks. It's time that I put a stop to this before I get some permanent scars, but how?
response:
I appreciate you sharing this. It takes a lot of courage to acknowledge what's happening and to decide that you want to make a change. Since you mentioned that the scratching often happens without you realizing it, finding ways to keep your hands busy or creating a physical barrier might be a helpful first step. Some people find it useful to wear long sleeves, use fidget toys, or keep their nails trimmed short to minimize the damage when the habit arises.

Because this is something you want to stop, reaching out to a healthcare professional or a therapist could be incredibly beneficial. They can help you explore any underlying stress or anxiety that might be triggering the scratching and work with you on habit-reversal techniques. Please remember to be gentle with yourself as you work through this process, and consider keeping your skin clean and cared for to help it heal.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response:
It sounds exhausting to carry rage that feels so much bigger than the situations that trigger it, and I want to acknowledge how much self-awareness it takes to observe that intensity without acting on it. The fact that you stay lucid and don't want to be consumed by resentment says something important about who you are.

Anger that's this disproportionate often has roots deeper than the immediate trigger—old wounds, unmet needs, or overwhelm that finds a release valve in the present moment. A therapist, especially one trained in approaches like DBT or trauma-informed work, can help you understand what's fueling it and build tools to manage the surges. If you ever feel you might genuinely lose control or harm yourself or someone else, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You deserve support in carrying this, and it's possible to loosen anger's grip.

prompt: How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?
response:
Counselors typically consider ending or transitioning care when a few things line up. The most common reason is progress: when you've met the goals you set together, developed coping skills, and feel more equipped to handle challenges on your own, that's often a natural point to wrap up. Termination is ideally a collaborative decision, discussed openly rather than announced suddenly.

There are other reasons too.
