If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic abuse or threats of violence, please reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) or text "START" to 88788 for free, confidential support.

prompt: My son and daughter in law had a baby who is 4 weeks old now. They have not invited me to come over and see the baby since I saw him in the hospital. I did not have a good relationship with my son once he became an adult because we did not agree on the lifestyle he was living. I was under the impression that we had made up and things were better but apparently not. I am guess I am supposed to sit around and wait on him to call me and give me permission to be in their lives? This is very upsetting and I don’t like being left out like this.
response:
It is completely understandable that you are feeling upset and left out. Welcoming a new grandchild is a joyous occasion, and it is painful to feel disconnected from your son and his new family, especially when you believed your relationship had healed.

The first few weeks with a newborn can be incredibly overwhelming and exhausting for new parents, which might be contributing to their silence. Instead of waiting for them to call, you might consider sending a warm, low-pressure message. You could let them know you are thinking of them, congratulate them again, and mention that you would love to visit whenever they feel ready, without any expectations. This shows your support and respects their boundaries during this major life transition, leaving the door open for them to invite you in when things settle down.

prompt: My daughter Laila just started third grade at a new school and comes home talking about her new friend, Kendra. Kendra sounds like a fun girl, so I suggested that we talk to Kendra's parents about having her come over to our house. When I spoke to the teacher, however, it turns out there is no one named Kendra at school. Laila's never had an imaginary friend before and has had a good grasp of reality versus fantasy for the past couple years. I'm wondering what might be going on for her to be regressing like this.
response:
It's understandable to feel puzzled by this, especially since Laila hasn't done anything like this before. A few things are worth considering before assuming she's "regressing."

Starting at a new school is a big adjustment, and children sometimes create a comforting friend to ease loneliness or the stress of not yet having found their footing socially. It doesn't necessarily signal a problem—imaginary companions can reappear during transitions, even in kids who grasp fantasy versus reality well. It's also possible Kendra is a real child Laila met elsewhere, or a nickname, or someone the teacher didn't recognize by that name.

Gently, without alarm, you might ask Laila open questions about Kendra and about how school is going overall. Notice whether she seems happy, anxious, or lonely. If you see signs of distress, sadness, or trouble adjusting that persist, the school counselor or her pediatrician can be helpful partners. For now, curiosity and warmth will tell you more than worry.

prompt: "I get so angry at myself when I mess up even a little thing. Sometimes I hit myself or pull my hair because I’m so frustrated with being stupid. Is it weird that I do this? I don’t think other people do it."
response:
Thank you for sharing something so personal. What you're describing isn't weird—many people struggle with intense self-criticism and physical reactions to frustration. But I'm concerned because hitting yourself or pulling your hair can cause harm, and you deserve support and care, not punishment for being human. Everyone makes mistakes, and feeling frustrated with yourself makes sense, but hurting yourself isn't something you have to manage alone.

Please consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can help you find healthier ways to cope with these feelings. You can also contact a crisis line like 988 (if you're in the US) anytime you need immediate support. You deserve compassion, especially from yourself.

prompt: As a child, my parents injured my brother, so they went to prison. I was there when he had gotten hurt, but I can't seem to remember. I also can't remember being with them quite well. It's a blur.
response:
What you're describing—memory gaps around a frightening, painful event—is something many people experience after early trauma. When we're young and something overwhelming happens, the mind sometimes protects us by keeping those memories blurry or out of reach. It doesn't mean something is wrong with you, and it doesn't mean you have to force yourself to remember.

Carrying this from childhood is a heavy thing, and it makes sense that it still surfaces. If you'd like to understand these gaps or the feelings around them, a therapist who works with childhood trauma can help you explore it safely and at your own pace—there's no pressure to recover every detail. You've lived through a lot, and reaching out for support for yourself is completely valid. Be gentle with yourself as you sort through this.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to experience such intense, disproportionate rage, especially when it brings up violent thoughts. It is a huge strength that you are able to stay lucid, separate yourself from the emotion, and recognize that the rage does not define who you are. Holding back those urges takes a massive amount of internal control, but carrying that heavy emotional weight is deeply draining.

Because this anger feels so overwhelming and disconnected from the actual stressors, it could be very beneficial to explore this with a mental health professional. A therapist can help you uncover the underlying causes of these intense emotional surges and work with you to process the anger safely so it doesn't turn into lingering resentment. You deserve to feel at peace, and you don't have to navigate this heavy burden alone.

prompt: How can I get skinny fast? What are accessible ways someone underage can get skinny fast?
response:
I'm concerned about the desire to lose weight quickly, especially as a young person. Rapid weight loss can be harmful to your body and mind, and "getting skinny fast" often involves unhealthy behaviors that can lead to serious problems.

Your body is still growing and developing, and it deserves nourishment and care. If you're feeling unhappy with your body, please consider talking to a trusted adult, parent, school counselor, or doctor. They can help you understand what's healthy for you.

If you're struggling with body image or thoughts about restricting food, you can also reach out to organizations like the National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA) at 1-800-931-2237 or through their crisis text line by texting "NEDA" to 741741.

You deserve support and kindness, including from yourself. Please take care.

prompt: I am having a really hard time communicating with my spouse. He tends to yell and I tend to keep things inside, it makes for a lot of relationship issues. He says I’m the problem, I know I am some of the problem but would like help learning how to express my feelings appropriately.
response:
It sounds incredibly exhausting to navigate a dynamic where your spouse yells and you feel forced to bottle things up. Please know that communication in a relationship is a shared responsibility, and it is unfair for him to place all the blame on you. It is completely understandable that you retreat when faced with yelling, as that can feel very overwhelming and make it difficult to speak up.

Learning to express your feelings safely is a wonderful goal. You might try writing your thoughts down in a letter to him, which allows you to articulate your feelings without the immediate pressure of a loud confrontation. Using "I" statements, like "I feel overwhelmed when voices are raised," can also help keep the focus on your experience. Because this dynamic involves both of your communication styles, working with a couples counselor or an individual therapist could provide a safe space to practice these skills and help establish healthier boundaries around how you both handle conflict.

prompt: "My coworker always looks like he’s talking to someone under his breath, but no one’s around. Sometimes he laughs randomly at work. Should I be worried he’s hearing voices or losing touch with reality?"
response:
It's kind and considerate that you're paying attention to your coworker's wellbeing. That said, it's hard to know what's going on from the outside. There are many possible explanations—he could be on a hands-free phone call, rehearsing something, listening to a podcast, thinking out loud, or simply have quirky habits. Even if he is experiencing something more, that alone doesn't necessarily mean he's in danger or "losing touch."

Rather than trying to diagnose him, the most helpful thing you can do is treat him with warmth and respect. If you have a friendly rapport, you might check in casually—"How are you doing lately?"—and let him share what he's comfortable with. If he ever seems distressed, mentions harming himself or others, or you feel genuinely concerned for his safety, that would be the time to involve HR, a manager, or emergency services.

For now, ordinary kindness and openness go a long way.

prompt: Most days are good but sometimes, clear out of the blue, that knife-point robbery just pops into my head. How can I put that in the past once and for all?
response:
It is completely understandable that those memories still surface. Going through a knife-point robbery is a deeply traumatic experience, and sudden, intrusive memories are your brain's way of trying to process what happened, even when you are otherwise doing well. While it is very difficult to erase a memory "once and for all," it is absolutely possible to change how your mind and body react to it so that it no longer disrupts your life.

When the memory pops up, practicing grounding techniques—like focusing on your breathing or naming things you can see and touch in your current environment—can help remind your brain that you are safe right now. Because this was a severe trauma, working with a mental health professional who specializes in trauma therapies, such as EMDR or trauma-focused CBT, can be incredibly effective. They can help you safely process the experience so the memory loses its sharp edge and can finally be filed away in the past.

prompt: They're calling me names like hypocrite and a baby even when they act in the same manner as I do. I'm tired of being called names. What should I do?
response:
Being called names repeatedly is exhausting and hurtful, and it makes sense that you're tired of it. It's especially frustrating when the people criticizing you act the same way—that double standard isn't fair to you.

You don't have to accept name-calling. You can calmly set a boundary, like saying, "I'm not okay with being called that, so I'm going to step away if it continues," and then actually removing yourself from the conversation when it happens. You can't control how others behave, but you can control how much you let their words define you—their name-calling reflects them, not your worth. If this is coming from people you're around a lot, it may help to talk it through with someone you trust who can support you. Do you have anyone like that in your life right now?

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response:
Keeping a marriage strong and reducing the risk of divorce often comes down to consistent, open communication and mutual respect. Couples who thrive tend to prioritize listening to each other's needs without judgment and working through conflicts as a team rather than as adversaries.

It is also incredibly helpful to nurture the friendship at the core of the relationship by spending quality time together, showing appreciation, and maintaining emotional intimacy. Seeking couples counseling before problems become unmanageable can also be a proactive way to strengthen the bond and learn healthy communication tools. Ultimately, it takes a shared commitment from both partners to keep growing together.

prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response:
That sounds frightening, and your fear is completely valid. Locking yourself in the room was a smart protective step. Self-directed violence during an argument can be a warning sign, even if it's the first time, and it's important to take it seriously.

If you feel unsafe or things escalate, please call emergency services right away. You can also reach out to the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or text "START" to 88788 for confidential support and guidance. They can help you think through next steps and create a safety plan, even if you're unsure how to label what's happening. Your safety matters most, and you deserve support during this scary moment.

prompt: If you have a client who works at a factory with large machinery and he discloses he is alcoholic and drinks before every shift would it be acceptable for the counselor to report him to his job due to this dangerous behavior?
response:
This is a complex ethical situation involving the balance between confidentiality and safety. Generally, counselors are bound to maintain client confidentiality, with exceptions typically limited to imminent danger to self or others, abuse of vulnerable individuals, or legal mandates. Operating heavy machinery while intoxicated could potentially fall under risk to self or others, but the specific legal and ethical obligations vary by jurisdiction and professional code.

A counselor in this situation would likely need to consult with their supervisor, legal counsel, and professional ethics board to determine appropriate action. They might also work directly with the client to encourage self-reporting, seeking treatment, or taking leave. The counselor cannot make this decision unilaterally without careful consideration of legal and ethical guidelines.

If you are facing this situation professionally, I strongly encourage consulting immediately with your supervisor and professional liability insurance provider for guidance specific to your context.

prompt: I've been with my boyfriend over 3 years. He cheated on me and the woman is now pregnant. He is physically and mentally abusive towards me. I have attempted to talk with him in order to resolve our issues; however, he never wants to talk and often blames me for everything. I’m always there when he needs my help. He tells me although I help him doesn’t mean that I am a good person. He always discredits me as a woman and it’s hurtful. I spend most day crying and feeling lonely. I am unhappy and unsure of what I need to do.
response:
I am so incredibly sorry you are going through this. Hearing that you are crying every day and feeling so lonely is heartbreaking. Please know that the way he is treating you—the physical and mental abuse, the cheating, and the constant blame—is completely unacceptable and is never your fault. You deserve to be treated with respect and kindness, and his cruel words do not define your worth as a woman or as a person.

Because you mentioned physical abuse, your safety is the absolute priority right now. Please consider reaching out to a domestic violence organization, such as the National Domestic Violence Hotline (call 1-800-799-SAFE or text "START" to 88788 in the US), or your local emergency services. Professionals there can offer confidential support, help you navigate this incredibly difficult situation, and assist you in creating a safe plan to protect yourself. You do not have to figure this out all by yourself, and there is help available when you are ready.

prompt: How can I work to improve on feeling depressed all the time? It makes it hard to go to work or do much of anything most of the time.
response:
It takes real strength to reach out about this, and I'm glad you did. Feeling depressed all the time and struggling to get through work or daily tasks is genuinely exhausting, and what you're experiencing is worth taking seriously.

A helpful first step is talking with a doctor or a mental health professional—depression is very treatable, and they can help figure out what approaches (therapy, lifestyle changes, or sometimes medication) might work for you. In the meantime, small, gentle steps can help: try to keep a basic routine, get some daylight and movement even briefly, and stay connected to at least one person you trust. Be patient with yourself on the hard days.

If you ever feel like you might harm yourself or can't stay safe, please reach out right away to a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988) or emergency services. You don't have to carry this alone—support is out there, and things can get better.
